Validation now applies in preview and all execution modes; richer inference remains distinct
Mapping rules build one structured activity output
Atomic independently scripted payload, attributes and named-variable targets
Streaming multiple targets use per-record JSON envelopes
Supported visual rules can generate and restore XSLT
Object-field synchronization and whole-expression graph nodes
Unsupported syntax is preserved; arbitrary code is not inferred as detailed field connections
Map & Test, saved cases, expected output comparison
Map & Test using the shared embedded engine
API-level preview verified; installed desktop mouse interaction not automated in this review
Bounded file-record execution and explicit batch helpers
Incremental JSON array/JSONL/CSV input and atomic file output
Not arbitrary live connector stream objects or all external reader/writer conventions
Not lossless conversion of arbitrary projects, modules or proprietary code

blocks.text: The stated boundaries remain real. Installing more function names or presenting a script as accepted would not make those semantics equivalent. Scripts using unsupported features should be migrated explicitly; do not treat an accepted small sample as proof that every input or external project is compatible.
Verification and performance

`backend/tests/test_transform_semantics.py` checks documented control-flow, collection and string behavior. `test_transform_execution_parity.py` checks eight independently reviewed cases through preview, Run, Debug and both generated archives, plus event-loop responsiveness. Existing Mapper tests cover schema, cardinality, repeated structures, bindings and archive behavior. Installed sample bindings are imported and exercised with `test_bw613_vendor_samples.py`; this executes their converted representation in MINA, not the installed vendor engine.

The benchmark runs an eight-field transformation of 100,000 approximately 1 KiB records with four workers, batches of 1,000 and a 600-second deadline per mode. Every output is checked against a separately constructed expected record, including trim/uppercase normalization and an array sum. Run/Debug log bookkeeping remains enabled. Generated archive startup, import, IPC and final cleanup are included. This common workload is narrower than the entire capability matrix and is not a long-duration memory soak or a comparison against another runtime.
Measured on 2026-11-16, all eight cases completed with 100,000 unique payloads verified per case (800,000 records total):

See the [aggregate evidence](validation/mapping-conformance-summary-2026-11-16.json) for exact values and individual report filenames. The original direct archive default-operation failure is retained in `validation/mapping-transformer-python-direct-before-default-export-fix-2026-11-16.json`. The shared harness's older reports use a generic Mapper scope label even for the Transformer workload; the `family` field selects the activity actually executed.
From the repository root with backend/test dependencies available:

python scripts/flow-throughput.py --family mapper --mode run --records 100000 --deadline 600 --output tmp/mapper-run.json --diagnostics tmp/mapper-run-logs
python scripts/flow-throughput.py --family transformer --mode run --records 100000 --deadline 600 --output tmp/transformer-run.json --diagnostics tmp/transformer-run-logs
Repeat each with `debug`, `python-direct` and `python-engine` and fresh output paths. No broker or network service is required. Keep temporary generated files out of Git.
Actual Kafka complete-flow qualification

This qualification uses actual Apache Kafka 3.9.1 in a fresh, single-node KRaft environment on this Windows development machine. It uses Kafka's real Java broker and the actual Python client, not a mock, emulator or substituted messaging service. The environment follows the [Apache Kafka KRaft quick start](https://kafka.apache.org/39/getting-started/quickstart/). The existing local `kafka_2.13-3.9.1.tgz` was checked against [Apache's published SHA-512 checksum](https://archive.apache.org/dist/kafka/3.9.1/kafka_2.13-3.9.1.tgz.sha512) and matched. No new broker distribution was downloaded or installed system-wide.
Workload and acceptance

Each of Run, Debug, direct Python archive and engine Python archive must finish 100,000 records in at most 600 seconds. Four concurrent task workers each use a separate fresh single-partition topic, with approximately 1 KiB per record and 1,000 records per task batch. Every record passes through a For-Each group and an eight-field Mapper, including trim, uppercase and sum transformations, then through a Kafka publish activity with delivery confirmation. A receive task reads the records back. Full payloads and unique sequence numbers are checked, including cross-branch isolation and missing/duplicate detection. Normal Run/Debug logging and final runtime/client cleanup remain enabled. Both archive tests generate and execute new archives in separate Python processes; generation, import, startup and IPC are included in their elapsed times.

The tests call the same WorkflowRuntime and DebugManager used by Studio. They do not automate mouse interaction with the installed Windows app or measure UI render latency. The receiver path tested here is Get; continuous receiver triggers, consumer rebalances, failover, transactions and multi-broker replication are outside this qualification. A fast 100,000-record test is not a long-duration soak or proof that every production topology will meet the same deadline.
Reproduce in another workspace

Keep `scripts/kafka-local-qa.py` and `scripts/flow-throughput.py` in Git. Do not copy temporary broker stores, generated applications or Python environments. Install the project's development dependencies, the `aiokafka` client (used by the direct archive and provisioning), `confluent-kafka` (used by the runtime) and `psutil` for the benchmark. Supply Java 17 and an extracted Apache Kafka 3.9 distribution, then run from the repository root:
python scripts/kafka-local-qa.py --kafka-home <extracted-kafka-home> --java <java-executable> --records 100000 --output-dir tmp/kafka-qualification-new

The helper launches only its own broker on loopback ports 29092/29093, creates new topics for every mode, runs the four existing complete-flow benchmarks sequentially and stops only its broker. It refuses occupied ports and existing report paths. Override `--port` and `--controller-port` together when necessary. Test-only PLAINTEXT listeners, replication factor one and 24-hour retention are deliberate local fixture settings; they do not qualify TLS/SASL or replicated deployments. Fresh storage avoids reopening old Windows Kafka indexes. Storage and private diagnostics remain under the ignored output directory for investigation; the helper does not delete previous test data or modify installed broker configuration.

Read each mode's JSON result and private diagnostic log when a test fails. A nonzero child exit or failed payload/deadline audit prevents a passing summary. The broker distribution is a local prerequisite and is not bundled with MINA.
Results
On 2026-11-16 all four modes passed with 100,000 unique full payloads verified in each mode (400,000 records in total):

The minimum required rate is 166.7 records/second. Run retained 701,800 log entries across completed task results; Debug retained 501,500 across those results. These counts are accumulated observations, not the number of entries resident at once. The environment used Java 17, Python 3.11.9, aiokafka 0.12.0 and confluent-kafka 2.16.1. Broker logs contained no ERROR/FATAL entries during these tests.

A 100-record smoke test also passed in all four modes. Thirty focused flow, messaging-throughput, sender-setting and connector regression tests passed. Launcher checks confirmed occupied-port refusal and existing-report preservation. The temporary broker was stopped and ports 29092/29093 were confirmed closed. No new runtime performance or correctness defect was found by this workload; no runtime code changes were necessary for this qualification.

See the [aggregate report](validation/kafka-actual-summary-2026-11-16.json) and its four linked per-mode report filenames for the sanitized measurements. Actual EMS qualification remains separate and blocked on its server distribution; Kafka results do not establish EMS or hosted Pub/Sub performance.
Pub/Sub throughput and temporary environment
Qualification scope

An official Google Pub/Sub emulator was provisioned locally because no GCP QA environment was available. This is a real gRPC/client-library integration test against Google's emulator, not an in-memory MINA message queue or mocked SDK speed test. It **does not qualify hosted GCP throughput**, IAM, service-account token refresh, TLS, regional network latency, quotas, failover or exactly-once delivery. Google's documented emulator limitations apply: [Testing locally](https://docs.cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/emulator).

Temporary environment: emulator component **0.8.38**, fetched from Google's SDK component manifest, archive SHA-256 `f55bde05f616816e44da6e237e82cd41b6e43ba0c6cdca7c479179681ebe1168`. The server bound only to `127.0.0.1:18085`, used project `mina-qa`, anonymous emulator credentials and fresh synthetic topics/subscriptions. No cloud project, billable resource or global credential/environment setting was created. Emulator binaries and private diagnostics remain under ignored `tmp/` and are not redistributed with MINA.
Measured results
Each complete flow processed and checked **100,000 records** within the **600-second limit**:

Four concurrent workers process 1,000-record task batches. The publish task executes Start → For-Each [eight-field Mapper → confirmed Publish] → End. A receive task executes Start → Pull → End, repeating for partial batches. Every sequence number and complete transformed payload is checked for missing records, duplication, corruption and wrong-branch routing. Run/Debug share the Studio-style runtime/debug manager. Archives execute their actual generated ZIP contents in four persistent processes. Timings include archive generation/import/startup where applicable, task orchestration, normal logging, SDK calls, IPC, full readback validation and cleanup. Browser rendering and control-plane persistence are excluded. This qualifies these batch Pull flows, not every schema or streaming/manual-ack starter topology.

The separate 10-minute soak used 32 concurrent confirmed send callers, 2,000-record cycles and a ten-second minimum cycle interval. It reached **100,000 fully verified records at 491.369 seconds** and counted **120,000 before the 600-second window ended**. Total duration was 600.382 seconds. Client creation/cleanup and audit are included; late cycles cannot satisfy the strict count gate. No forced garbage collection was used. Endpoint RSS growth alone cannot establish absence of all leaks.

Results: `docs/validation/pubsub-emulator-*-2026-11-16.json`. The initial Debug cleanup-fixture failure is retained separately and excluded from qualification. The harness now marks a completed session as stopping before awaiting native cleanup, matching Studio Stop ordering, so bounded history cannot evict it mid-cleanup. Retention settings remain enabled.
Runtime and export changes

Confirmed sends await real SDK futures through asyncio instead of occupying shared executor threads for the duration of network acknowledgement. This preserves message IDs, confirmation and error propagation. Timeout/cancellation does not cancel an uncertain underlying send; late exceptions are consumed. Rare uncached one-shot clients retain their existing synchronous completion/cleanup path.

Direct Python publisher enqueueing runs off its event loop. Its message/byte flow-control limits use bounded SDK backpressure, matching the engine settings; the regional endpoint override is passed to the SDK. Defaults for queued versus confirmed completion are unchanged.

Direct Pull now acknowledges received records in Auto mode. Previously unacknowledged records could be redelivered and consume throughput. Explicit Client/manual modes are not auto-acknowledged; application acknowledgement handling remains required and is outside this qualification.

Pull batching respects the service's 1,000-message response limit, and Direct Pull honors the configured receive timeout. Source/engine accept fully qualified topic/subscription paths without prefixing them twice. See [Pub/Sub limits](https://docs.cloud.google.com/pubsub/quotas) and [Pull semantics](https://docs.cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/reference/rest/v1/projects.subscriptions/pull).

No delivery default was changed to obtain these results. This test requests confirmation for each publish and audits readback; buffered enqueueing alone is not counted as delivered work. Subscriber clients retain their existing per-Pull/manual-ack ownership behavior; no shared subscriber cache was introduced.
Reproducing a temporary environment

Use an appropriate Java runtime, MINA backend dependencies, Google Pub/Sub Python client and the benchmark's test-only `psutil` dependency. Obtain the official emulator JAR through the Google Cloud SDK component installer or its official component manifest. Do not commit the downloaded emulator binary.

The reusable launcher owns its emulator process, creates unique topics/subscriptions, runs all four modes, deletes completed-case resources and restores its process environment. It refuses to reuse an occupied port or stop another server. A supplied JAR is required; the launcher does not install system-wide software.
python scripts/pubsub-emulator-qa.py --jar PATH_TO_OFFICIAL_EMULATOR_JAR --java PATH_TO_JAVA --port 18085 --records 100000 --workers 4 --soak-seconds 600 --output-dir tmp/pubsub-qa
Smoke check of the launcher and all four modes:
python scripts/pubsub-emulator-qa.py --jar PATH_TO_OFFICIAL_EMULATOR_JAR --java PATH_TO_JAVA --port 18086 --records 10 --workers 1 --soak-seconds 0 --output-dir tmp/pubsub-smoke

For hosted GCP qualification, use approved dedicated QA topics/subscriptions with the protected profile formats and flow commands from `COMPLETE_FLOW_THROUGHPUT.md`. Remove `PUBSUB_EMULATOR_HOST`, supply normal GCP authentication, and rerun the same exact count/deadline gates. Never infer hosted performance from emulator timings or consume business subscriptions during an audit.

pages.title: JMS batch Get reuse and strict soak qualification

blocks.text: JMS batch Get reuse and strict soak qualification

The target is at least **100,000 persistent-send/readback records fully audited before the 600-second soak window ends**. This is stronger than the earlier paced correctness soak, which processed 92,000 roundtrips over approximately 605 seconds. Records finishing after the new window are excluded from its acceptance count.
Measured results

The strict soak passed: **100,000 verified roundtrips by 589.394 seconds**. The complete run ended at 603.155 seconds with 102,000 records audited; the final 2,000 records were excluded from the deadline-qualified count. The prior comparable lifecycle soak audited only 92,000 records over about 605 seconds.
Complete flows, 100,000 records each (limit 600 seconds):

Profiles, timing limits and the actual-provider qualification boundary below are part of these results. Rates are workload/host-specific, not a universal production SLA. Reports and the final matrix are `docs/validation/jms-optimized-*-2026-11-16.json`.
Provider authentication

Studio, Run, Debug and both Python formats allow provider/factory defaults when both JMS username and password are blank. The Java bridge calls the provider's no-argument `createConnection()` in that case. If either credential is supplied, both configured values are passed unchanged to `createConnection(username, password)`. Authentication remains enforced by the provider; optional fields do not grant access to a secured broker.

JNDI uses its provider URL and connection-factory name instead of requiring an unused direct connection URL. Naming credentials are optional unless the naming provider requires them. Set the provider’s initial context factory for either EMS or JMS. Rebuild the matching Java bridge and restart Studio to load this change.
Connection reuse

Batch Gets (`maxMessages > 1`) reuse a bounded, scope-isolated Java worker, physical provider connection and auto-acknowledge session. Previously each Get started a JVM and established a new connection. A separate receive-worker cache identity prevents a waiting receive from occupying the sender's worker/session. The existing eight-worker sender budget is preserved, with a separate four-worker batch-Get budget. Receive fanout cannot exhaust publisher cache capacity; excess configurations within each role retain the one-shot fallback. Idle reaping, application/Debug Stop and process cleanup release workers.
Connections with an explicit JMS `clientId` retain one-shot Get ownership, respecting provider-wide client-ID uniqueness/lifetime rules. The qualification profile does not configure a client ID.

Receive cache identity includes destination, selector and queue/topic/JNDI mode. A waiting Get on an empty destination/filter therefore does not occupy a different destination/filter's cached session. The role-specific bounds and one-shot fallback still apply.

Each Get creates its own consumer, applies that call's destination and selector, and **closes the consumer before returning**. It does not keep an active consumer holding prefetched messages between calls. Every batch retains its original total receive timeout and bounded maximum of 10,000 messages. The default single-message Get and request/reply still use the original one-shot path. Persistent send settings, priority/TTL reset, acknowledgement defaults and ordering of calls on a session are preserved. Uncertain sends or receives are never automatically replayed after bridge failure.

`receiverReused` identifies subsequent batch Gets served by an existing receiver worker. Existing `body`, headers, properties, messages and count remain available. Receive-only Run applications now participate in application/shutdown worker cleanup too.

Both Python formats include the updated Python bridge support. **Rebuild the Java bridge with the matching source** when rebuilding Studio or deploying the archives; an older bridge lacks the receive RPC command. Normal provider driver and complete Java runtime prerequisites still apply.
Test workload

The strict activity soak uses real loopback Artemis JMS 2.40.0, persistent sends, approximately 1 KiB records, eight concurrent send callers, 2,000 records per cycle and Gets of up to 1,000. Its existing ten-second minimum cycle interval remains in place. Every payload and sequence number is checked for corruption, duplication, omission and cross-run contamination. The benchmark includes cycle startup, teardown and readback. A cycle contributes to `verifiedWithinWindow` only when its complete audit and cleanup have finished by 600 seconds. The final cycle may finish later, but cannot inflate the acceptance count.

Complete flows independently execute Start → For-Each [eight-field Mapper → persistent Send] → End, then Start → batch Get → End with exact payload auditing. Four workers process a shared total of 100,000 records. Run/Debug share the Studio-style runtime/debug manager. Each archive is generated, imported and run in four persistent worker processes. Archive generation/startup, task orchestration, input generation, IPC, payload checks and shutdown are inside each full-flow timer. The limit is 600 seconds per mode.

These are automated runtime/Debug engine tests, not browser rendering or control-plane persistence tests. Other schemas, single-record flows, receiver-starter dispatch, TLS, failover and different provider/network topologies require their own qualification. The local broker is **Artemis JMS, not the actual EMS provider**. The shared code supports both MINA activity types, but actual EMS throughput remains unverified without an approved EMS QA connection and queues.
Reproduction

Use the dedicated private profiles documented in `SENDER_PERFORMANCE.md` and `COMPLETE_FLOW_THROUGHPUT.md`, with fresh queues for independent runs. Never use business queues. Rebuild the Java bridge first using the normal Studio/sidecar build, or compile its source into the configured test bridge classes directory. Use the normal provider driver directory and Java executable settings.

python scripts/activity-throughput.py --family jms --operation publish --config PRIVATE.json --records 2000 --batch-size 1000 --concurrency 8 --soak-seconds 600 --cycle-interval 10 --minimum-soak-records 100000 --output SOAK.json
python scripts/flow-throughput.py --family jms --mode run --config PRIVATE_FOUR_QUEUES.json --records 100000 --workers 4 --batch-size 1000 --deadline 600 --output FLOW.json --diagnostics PRIVATE_LOG_DIRECTORY

Repeat the flow command for `debug`, `python-direct` and `python-engine`. Use `--family ems` and the actual approved EMS provider configuration to qualify that provider; local JMS results are not a substitute. The runtime soak now fails explicitly if its minimum record count is not reached inside the requested window.

Native contract tests compile the real Java bridge with a disposable JMS fixture. They check reuse, per-call consumer closure/selector handling, independent sender/receiver pools and no replay on receive error. These offline cases establish correctness, not live provider performance. Reports are under `docs/validation/jms-optimized-*-2026-11-16.json`.
The pre-isolation Run result and a stopped-broker fixture failure are retained separately for traceability and excluded from the final matrix.
Activity circuit breakers

Use **Activity → Advanced → Activity circuit breaker** on an outbound database, messaging, file-transfer or SAP activity to give a failing dependency time to recover. The policy starts disabled. HTTP, REST and SOAP keep their existing transport settings. Listener, reply and settlement activities keep their normal execution paths.
Enable the breaker and set the threshold and recovery delay. The defaults are
five failures and 30 seconds.
Optionally enter fault types, codes or exception class names to count. A
blank filter counts all ordinary failures. Use observed connector fault names when business or validation errors should leave the breaker unchanged.
Add an Error transition or select a Catch handler for `CircuitOpen`. The

existing activity Errors policy can also return the fault or continue with the previous value. Run and Debug log when a breaker opens, blocks an attempt or closes after recovery. Debug follows the same task-level Catch handlers as Run. Enable **Pause on Error** to inspect the fault before the handler runs.

Each qualifying connector attempt counts, including activity retries. A successful attempt clears the counter. The attempt that reaches the threshold retains its original fault and stops retrying. Later calls raise `CircuitOpen` before contacting the connector. After the recovery delay, one call probes the dependency. A successful probe closes the circuit and a qualifying failure starts another cooldown. Cancellation releases a probe slot. Calls already in flight finish under their connector's own timeout and cannot close a circuit that opened after they started.

State is in memory per runtime instance, project, execution mode, environment, task and activity. Use separate activities for dependencies that must fail independently. Debug and Run use independent circuits. Both Python archives apply the same policy across task invocations within the life of the Python process. Separate workers apply independent limits. Each registry bounds its state to 4,096 circuits and reclaims inactive entries after one hour as needed. If every slot is occupied, new protected activities raise `CircuitBreakerCapacity` through the existing fault path.
See the [circuit breaker pattern](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/circuit-breaker) for the relationship between retries and recovery probes.
Sender performance investigation — 16 November 2026
For subsequent Pub/Sub fixes and official-emulator full-flow/soak qualification, see [Pub/Sub throughput](PUBSUB_THROUGHPUT.md). Hosted GCP performance remains a separate qualification.

For the subsequent batch-Get optimization and deadline-qualified 100,000-record soak, see [JMS batch reuse](JMS_BATCH_REUSE.md). This page and its original reports retain the earlier measurement scope.

Sender rates depend on delivery semantics, round-trip latency, persistence, payload size and concurrency. A buffered enqueue rate must not be presented as broker delivery throughput. The sender benchmark waits for final Kafka flush and independently verifies every complete payload, including missing/duplicate detection. EMS/JMS persistent sends retain provider completion semantics. Pub/Sub live results require an approved cloud topic/subscription; local SDK tests do not qualify cloud throughput.
Changes and verification

`activity-throughput.py --confirm-delivery` now supports Kafka confirmation on **each** send. Without it, Kafka buffers normally but final flush and full readback are still required. `perSendConfirmation` explicitly records this distinction in the report. Use `--concurrency 1` to measure a serial sender and compare with the same workload at concurrency eight.

Pub/Sub's explicit batch delay `0` was incorrectly replaced by the 10 ms default through truthiness checks. Runtime, SDK client construction and Direct Python now preserve that override, using MINA's existing 1 ms minimum. Missing/empty settings still default to 10 ms. An activity override of zero takes precedence over a shared connection setting. Authentication, delivery confirmation and persistence defaults are unchanged.

Three regression tests validate the zero-delay behavior through runtime configuration, actual SDK BatchSettings and the generated-adapter implementation. These are offline correctness tests, not measurements of Pub/Sub service capacity.

Fresh real loopback Kafka topics and a real Artemis JMS queue are used. Reports are `docs/validation/sender-*-2026-11-16.json`. The earlier complete-flow qualification remains documented in `COMPLETE_FLOW_THROUGHPUT.md`; the new measurements isolate sender behavior and do not substitute for those flow measurements. Artemis JMS is not vendor EMS. Actual EMS and Pub/Sub need dedicated QA connection profiles and the affected project/task to reproduce the reported slow integration.

The initial Kafka fixture failed on restart while Windows held an old retention index open. That attempt did not produce a sender qualification. A new empty test data directory was formatted instead of modifying production configuration or deleting old data. Test-only retention covers the entire soak window.
Diagnosing slow projects
Record Run versus Debug, payload bytes, observed records/second, destination, environment, confirmation settings and number of active jobs. Use a dedicated test destination.

For Kafka, inspect activity `publisherQueueMs`, `producerSetupMs`, `sendAndWaitMs` and `publishLatencyMs`. Repeated setup time suggests dynamic connection/producer settings or lifecycle churn. A high confirmation time with low queue/setup time points toward the broker/network/acknowledgement path. Do not disable broker acknowledgements to hide a delivery problem.

For EMS/JMS, inspect `publishTiming.queueMs`, `bridgeMs`, `totalMs` and native `providerSendMs`. Provider persistence/round trips, sender queue contention and repeated Java-worker creation have different remedies. Per-record new Debug sessions can pay startup/cleanup costs that a single For-Each task session avoids. Retain persistent delivery where the integration requires it.

For Pub/Sub, serial confirmed sends may pay batching delay plus network/service latency on every record. Choose the batching delay and concurrency intentionally. Buffered publishing changes when the activity returns; use it only when the flow accepts queued completion and delivery is verified separately. The delay fix does not remove network or provider latency.

Avoid changing shared connection/producer options per record unless required: those settings define client cache identity. Keep normal authentication/TLS and delivery requirements during qualification.
Repeatable test commands

Use the protected dedicated-resource profile format from `MESSAGING_THROUGHPUT.md`. For a fresh single-partition Kafka topic, start at offset zero. Use a new topic for each independent case or set the exact protected `startOffset` for the synthetic test records. Never consume a business topic as an audit step.

python scripts/activity-throughput.py --family kafka --operation publish --config PRIVATE.json --records 100000 --concurrency 1 --confirm-delivery --output SERIAL.json
python scripts/activity-throughput.py --family kafka --operation publish --config PRIVATE.json --records 100000 --concurrency 8 --confirm-delivery --output PARALLEL.json
python scripts/activity-throughput.py --family kafka --operation publish --config PRIVATE.json --records 100000 --concurrency 8 --output BUFFERED.json
python scripts/activity-throughput.py --family kafka --operation publish --config PRIVATE.json --records 1000 --concurrency 8 --confirm-delivery --soak-seconds 600 --cycle-interval 5 --output SOAK.json

The paced soak repeats fully verified send/readback cycles and closes clients between cycles. It measures sustained correctness and lifecycle churn; it is not an unpaced maximum-capacity test. Final RSS comparisons alone do not prove absence of all leaks. SDKs, broker configuration and network geography can change results substantially.
Complete-flow throughput qualification

The target is **100,000 correctly transformed and delivered records within 600 seconds of total wall-clock time**, including task orchestration. This is stricter than the earlier activity-only send/receive timings in `MESSAGING_THROUGHPUT.md`. There is no extrapolation from a smaller workload.
Workload and execution modes
`scripts/flow-throughput.py` builds ordinary MINA project/task definitions:
A publish task runs Start → For-Each [Mapper → Publish/Send] → End.
A receive task runs Start → Get/Pull → End, repeated if the provider returns a partial batch.

Every received payload is checked against the expected transformed object. Missing records, duplicates, corruption, wrong-branch records, task failures, unsuccessful archive shutdown or elapsed time above 600 seconds fail the case.

Four concurrent workers each use a distinct dedicated destination. Each worker processes batches of 1,000 through the complete tasks. The publish task executes eight mappings for **every** record, including trim/uppercase and summation. Messages are approximately 1 KiB. Publishing requests broker delivery confirmation. Each worker completes its send task and receive/audit task before beginning its next batch. Workers share the total 100,000-record workload; this is not 100,000 per worker.

The standalone Mapper workload uses Start → For-Each [Mapper] → End, returns the accumulated batch and checks all transformed records. It exercises group iteration, accumulation and End input mapping as well as Mapper execution.
**Run:** `WorkflowRuntime.run`, including normal activity/group logging, transition scheduling, configuration/mapping resolution and task state. All concurrent jobs share one runtime, as in Studio.

**Debug:** `DebugManager.start` and resume through completion, with normal Debug logs/history, group scheduling, task state and session cleanup. Concurrent sessions share the Studio-style runtime/debug manager. There are no manual breakpoint pauses.
**Direct Python:** four persistent worker processes execute a generated ZIP via `application.main.run_task`. The actual exported tasks, groups, Mapper and connectors run in those processes.
**Engine Python:** the same process/ZIP execution pattern using the Engine Python export.

The wall clock starts before archive generation/import and worker startup, and ends after final client/process cleanup. It includes input generation, orchestration, send, receive, IPC and exact record validation. Broker provisioning, designer editing, installer construction, browser rendering, periodic Studio status HTTP polling and control-plane transport/persistence are outside this measurement. No activity methods are substituted for complete task execution, and no production logging/caching settings are disabled to obtain a pass.

These are representative batch flows, not a qualification of every possible integration, schema or receiver-starter dispatch pattern. Mapper target XSD validation, authentication/TLS overhead, broker failover and downstream business processing are not part of this workload. Archive results use **four worker processes**; they do not establish the same rate for one serial archive process.
Providers and results
Measured seconds for 100,000 records (limit: 600 seconds per case):
All 12 local cases passed, with every expected payload verified. These results apply to four concurrent workers and 1,000-record task batches. They are not serial single-worker guarantees.

The Kafka Engine archive initially took 372.7 seconds. Replacing timer-based acknowledgement waits with a native poll requesting at most 1 ms produced a final 66.6-second run, while retaining per-record delivery confirmation. Run and Debug also remain below the limit. Runs shared the host with other tests, so this is observed qualification evidence rather than a controlled hardware-normalized speedup claim.

Machine-readable results are `docs/validation/flow-<family>-<mode>-2026-11-15.json`; the final matrix is in `flow-summary-2026-11-15.json`. Only final reports containing all 100,000 verified records and a successful full elapsed-time check qualify. Reports with an `initial` suffix are retained measurement-development evidence and are not the final Studio-runtime qualification.

Kafka uses a real loopback Apache Kafka 3.9.1 broker with dedicated single-partition topics. JMS uses a real loopback Apache ActiveMQ Artemis 2.40.0 broker and persistent sends. **Artemis JMS is not vendor EMS.** GCP Pub/Sub and actual EMS require protected approved QA profiles and dedicated resources before their live full-flow target can be verified. Local test doubles are never used as throughput evidence.
Reproduction

Use a Python environment containing MINA's backend dependencies and the selected provider SDK. The Direct Kafka archive also needs its normal optional `aiokafka` dependency. For JMS/EMS, configure the complete Java bridge and the actual provider's driver directory using normal deployment settings. Do not commit private profiles or diagnostics.
The shared benchmark host helper also requires the test-only `psutil` package. Install it in the test environment; it is not a new MINA runtime dependency.
Example protected Kafka/JMS/EMS profile:

Use the selected provider's normal connection object, not Kafka settings for a JMS/EMS connection. Pre-provision a distinct Kafka topic per worker. For a fresh single-partition topic use starting offset zero; otherwise supply the exact starting offsets for **these synthetic test records**. Fresh destinations per mode avoid mixing earlier runs. For Pub/Sub also supply a `subscriptions` array with one dedicated pre-created subscription for each corresponding topic, and the normal project/authentication configuration. Get/Pull consumes and acknowledges data, so business destinations must never be used.

python scripts/flow-throughput.py --family kafka --mode run --config PRIVATE.json --records 100000 --workers 4 --batch-size 1000 --deadline 600 --output RESULT.json --diagnostics PRIVATE_LOG_DIRECTORY
python scripts/flow-throughput.py --family jms --mode debug --config PRIVATE.json --records 100000 --workers 4 --batch-size 1000 --deadline 600 --output RESULT.json --diagnostics PRIVATE_LOG_DIRECTORY
python scripts/flow-throughput.py --family mapper --mode python-direct --records 100000 --output RESULT.json --diagnostics PRIVATE_LOG_DIRECTORY

Repeat with `--mode run`, `debug`, `python-direct` and `python-engine`. Use `--family ems` with the actual EMS provider to qualify EMS, or `pubsub` with actual cloud resources. A pass for a different provider is not sufficient. The final JSON excludes connection values and raw provider errors; protected diagnostic files retain errors needed for investigation.
Run the harness correctness tests with `backend` on `PYTHONPATH`:
python -m unittest discover -s backend/tests -p test_flow_throughput.py

Those small memory-broker tests verify measurement behavior and error detection; actual generated Mapper ZIP execution is also tested. Their speed is not used in the live 100,000-record qualification.
Messaging and Mapper throughput qualification

The acceptance target is **100,000 records per direction within 600 seconds**, or at least 166.67 records/second. Lower elapsed time is better. Results are workload- and environment-specific; this is not a universal performance guarantee.

For the subsequent **complete-flow** qualification, including task orchestration and 100,000-record archive execution, see [Complete-flow throughput](COMPLETE_FLOW_THROUGHPUT.md). The activity-only and small compatibility reports below retain their original scope and are historical evidence, rather than the final full-flow matrix.
Reproducible workload

`scripts/activity-throughput.py` calls MINA's actual `WorkflowRuntime.execute` send and Get activities against dedicated broker resources. Each message is a 1,024-byte JSON payload containing a unique run identifier, sequence number and padding. Eight concurrent send calls are used; receives request batches of up to 1,000. Every record is independently read back and its complete payload checked for corruption, duplication and missing sequence numbers. Kafka publishing includes a successful delivery flush; it does not count enqueueing alone as completed delivery. Pub/Sub publishing explicitly requests delivery confirmation. Seeding is outside the receive timer; readback is outside the publish timer.

These activity benchmarks exclude the Studio UI, whole-task graph orchestration, execution-log collection, downstream business work and network latency beyond the local broker. They do not measure persistent receiver-starter dispatch, individual-record latency, failover or TLS authentication overhead. A batch Get result is not a measurement of 100,000 independently launched Get activities.

Mapper uses eight mappings, including trim/uppercase, sum, direct paths and nested targets, on approximately 1 KiB records. Every result is checked. Target XSD validation is not enabled in that workload; complex schemas, loops, XSLT and larger documents require separate capacity tests.
Runtime changes

Kafka Get performs its blocking provider work outside the asyncio event loop. It waits for the first record and drains immediately available records, instead of paying a complete timeout for every empty slot. Consumer setup/decoding failures close the consumer; manual confirmation retains ownership until confirmation.

Generated Kafka publishers honor an explicitly selected partition for buffered and confirmed sends. The qualification fixture pins both send and receive to partition zero; otherwise an auto-created multi-partition topic can make a one-partition read miss the published record.

EMS/JMS Get accepts `maxMessages` from 1 to 10,000, defaulting to one for existing projects. One total receive timeout bounds the batch. `body` and legacy headers refer to the first record; `messages` and `count` expose the complete batch. Run and generated Python adapters retain all received bodies. Use batching to amortize Java bridge startup; default single-message Gets do not meet the stated throughput target on this test host.

Shared native listeners wake the asyncio consumer when a delivery arrives, replacing a fixed 50 ms polling sleep. Cancellation removes its waiter without abandoning a blocked executor thread. This is correctness-tested; a high-rate receiver-starter SLA is not yet qualified.

Pub/Sub cached publishers no longer reconstruct service-account credentials/private keys before reusing the cached client. Authentication validation still happens when a new client is created. Pull is recognized as a receive operation, runs blocking provider work outside the event loop, and closes failed receives. Manual confirmation retains the subscriber until its last acknowledgement. These changes are regression-tested but require actual cloud measurement before a throughput claim.
Results and scope

Machine-readable reports are in `docs/validation/throughput-*-2026-11-15.json`. The Kafka broker is Apache Kafka 3.9.1 on loopback. JMS tests use Apache ActiveMQ Artemis 2.40.0 with persistent sends and the JMS bridge. **Artemis is not vendor EMS**. Live GCP Pub/Sub and vendor EMS require approved QA connections and dedicated topics/subscriptions/queues; their 100,000-record targets remain unverified.

The JMS pre-change baseline of 20 single-message Gets took 32.03 seconds. That small baseline is diagnostic evidence, not an acceptance test. The 1,000-record Kafka baseline is likewise not the 100,000-record qualification.

Mapper completed a continuous 600-second soak, processing and checking 4,995,087 records. Its first 100,000 took 11.491 seconds (8,702.7 records/second). Final process RSS was essentially unchanged (-0.016 MiB); this endpoint comparison alone does not prove absence of all leaks.

Kafka's 100,000 confirmed publishes took 24.036 seconds (4,160.5/second). Receiving and checking those records took 3.208 seconds (31,176.8/second). See the separate paced-soak report for sustained cycling; a paced soak is not an unpaced maximum-capacity measurement.

The Kafka paced soak completed 120 verified send/readback cycles over 601.03 seconds: 120,000 records checked, no record failures, and +2.66 MiB final RSS. Local JMS confirmed 100,000 persistent sends in 433.727 seconds (230.56/second), then received and checked them in 205.504 seconds (486.61/second), using batches of 1,000. Final RSS growth was +1.75 MiB. Both directions met the separate 600-second target. Their combined sequential elapsed time exceeds 600 seconds; this does not establish a simultaneous end-to-end task SLA.

The final small live round-trip compatibility checks passed for Kafka and JMS in Run, Debug, Direct Python and Engine Python. These checks execute generated applications, but are not 100,000-record archive benchmarks. Earlier failed compatibility reports are retained with `multipartition-fixture` and `partition-routing` suffixes; the first exposed a fixture mismatch and the follow-up identified the generated publisher's missing explicit-partition handling. Use the unsuffixed final report for the corrected results.
Running against dedicated QA resources
Create a protected JSON file outside Git:

Use the corresponding shared connection configuration for Kafka or EMS/JMS. For Pub/Sub, provision the subscription before publishing, use the same project and supply normal ADC or protected service-account configuration. The benchmark publishes synthetic messages and consumes/acknowledges them. Never point it at business traffic.

python scripts/activity-throughput.py --family pubsub --operation publish --config PRIVATE.json --records 100000 --concurrency 32 --batch-size 1000 --output RESULT.json
python scripts/activity-throughput.py --family ems --operation receive --config PRIVATE.json --records 100000 --batch-size 1000 --output RESULT.json
python scripts/activity-throughput.py --family mapper --operation map --records 100000 --soak-seconds 600 --output RESULT.json

Both broker-direction timings are recorded in a single run. Confirm that **both** are within 600 seconds. `passed` evaluates the selected `--operation`. A receive-only run still publishes its own unique data first, so no pre-existing business messages are consumed intentionally.

For a paced broker soak, add `--records 1000 --soak-seconds 600 --cycle-interval 5`. The same queue/subscription is reused after verified consumption; Kafka uses a single-partition dedicated topic and advances its custom offset between cycles. Set protected profile `startOffset` if the dedicated topic is not initially empty. Report duration includes client cleanup and pacing. No forced garbage collection is performed.

Run offline regressions with `python -m unittest discover -s backend/tests -p test_messaging_throughput.py`, with `backend` on `PYTHONPATH`. These test doubles protect behavior and do not establish cloud or vendor throughput.
Live messaging verification
What was actually exercised

Real Kafka 3.9.1 and Artemis 2.40.0 broker processes were started in an isolated temporary directory. They listened on loopback test ports with dedicated topics and queues; existing project destinations were not used. Kafka, JMS and AMQP 1.0 each passed a real round trip in Run, Debug, Direct Python and Engine Python: twelve checks in total. The exported applications were run through their command-line entry points, including connector shutdown.

This verifies JMS against Artemis, **not vendor EMS**. It also does not verify Google Cloud Pub/Sub, SAP, RabbitMQ AMQP 0.9.1, Azure Service Bus, SASL/TLS variants, clustered failover or maximum throughput. Those need the corresponding environments and dedicated approved test resources. A saved connection alone does not identify which existing business destinations may be used for a soak.

The local setup follows the [Kafka KRaft quickstart](https://kafka.apache.org/39/getting-started/quickstart/). [Artemis](https://artemis.apache.org/) supplies the real JMS/AMQP test broker. Their binary distributions were checked against the official SHA-512 files and kept under ignored `tmp/`; no broker binaries or downloaded SDKs were added to the repository or installer.
Issues found and fixed

AMQP 1.0 sends passed `None` to Proton's TTL setter, which failed even with default options. No-expiration sends now omit TTL, and positive expiration values convert activity milliseconds to Proton seconds.

AMQP receive passed an unsupported `auto_accept` keyword to the blocking client. Automatic receive now explicitly settles the received delivery. Manual acceptance/rejection uses the blocking SDK's argument-free methods and closes owned resources afterwards.
Only an actual Proton timeout means no message. Other receive failures now propagate as adapter faults instead of being hidden as an empty queue.
Absent AMQP content-type/correlation fields are omitted from the SDK constructor instead of being explicitly passed as `None`.
Kafka consumers no longer inherit the producer-only request-timeout setting that emitted a native warning on every polling operation.

Direct export specialization now normalizes Kafka Send/Get and Pub/Sub Subscribe aliases before selecting code. Previously it could remove the receive/pull branch and fail with `Unsupported Kafka operation: receive` in a real exported application.
Direct Kafka receive now honors the configured initial offset policy and custom partition/seek options. Consumer startup is inside its cleanup scope.

The Pub/Sub custom-CA credential wrapper preserves Google's SDK constructor/copy contract for scope, JWT-access and quota-project copies. Wrapper types are bounded to 32 cached combinations. An explicitly created TLS transport closes if client construction fails. These changes are verified with the installed Google SDK and local failure injection, **not live cloud authentication**.

SAP soak instrumentation now retains at most 10,000 latency samples and 1,000 error samples, with separate total counters and exact running min/mean/max. This is an instrumentation correction; it is not evidence of a live SAP test.
Scoped Java process termination now waits after a forced kill. Java timeout errors report the configured budget rather than a negative remaining timeout exposed by Windows after an interruption.
Sustained-load evidence and its limit

The first unpaced run stopped after 169 measured seconds, following 60 seconds of warmup. It completed 18,482 Kafka, 10,460 AMQP and 209 JMS round trips before a connection failure. It did **not** pass duration/error gates. Native connection errors occurred across the local brokers during the high-churn workload; Windows ephemeral-port pressure is a hypothesis, not a confirmed root cause or a fixed production issue. The failed result is retained in `docs/validation/live-messaging-first-pass-2026-11-14.json`.

A later bounded-rate attempt and its two archive attempts failed when the temporary Windows Kafka broker shut down. With logging enabled, recovery reproduced a retention-cleanup failure renaming a locked `.index` file, followed by all log directories being marked failed. The retained diagnostic is `docs/validation/kafka-windows-storage-failure-2026-11-14.txt`; failed reports include `live-messaging-broker-failure-2026-11-14.json` and both `live-messaging-archive-*-first-pass-2026-11-14.json` files. This establishes a broker storage failure for that later outage; it does not prove the cause of the earlier unpaced AMQP failure.

The final attempt uses a fresh temporary Kafka data directory, test-only retention of one day and a 1 GiB per-partition byte threshold, outside this small test workload. No existing broker data was deleted and no production retention setting was changed. This avoids exercising the failing Windows retention path; it does not fix or qualify that broker path. Production Kafka storage, retention and failover still require qualification on the target platform.

The final sustained run uses six workers, 60 seconds of warmup, 1,800 measured seconds, and a minimum cycle interval of one second per worker. That caps each worker at one round trip per second; JVM-based JMS may be slower. Its result is `docs/validation/live-messaging-2026-11-15.json`. A pass at this declared load does not resolve or qualify the unpaced high-rate failure.

The runner checks sent/received tokens, duration, unexpected errors, client RSS growth, late RSS slope, handles and threads. It samples child-process counts and RSS separately. Client gates are at most 128 MiB RSS growth, 0.5 MiB/minute late RSS slope, 24 additional handles and 8 additional threads. It does not force garbage collection. Broker RSS, disk growth and child-process resource trends must also be reviewed; the client gates alone are not complete server qualification. Counts include warmup. Latency retention is bounded.

The November 14 attempts were interrupted and remain failed. Windows power events were present during that test window, and sampled activity stopped well before the requested continuous duration even though wall-clock elapsed times grew to roughly an hour. Final continuous attempts are recorded under `2026-11-15` filenames. On Windows the runner now holds a temporary thread-scoped system execution request during the test and restores the prior state on exit; it does not change the power plan or require the display to remain on. A new continuity gate requires samples near both ends of the requested measurement window and rejects sample gaps exceeding 60 seconds. Manual suspension or infrastructure interruption still invalidates a run.
Running against approved QA resources

Keep a resolved connection configuration in a protected local JSON file outside Git. Supply one dedicated pre-created destination per worker; do not use business topics, queues or subscriptions. The runner does not delete or purge remote resources. A Kafka destination must be a fresh single-partition topic for offset-zero sequential checks. AMQP queues must exist before the first send; a broker may accept a message to an address with no queue and discard it according to its routing policy.

Supported round-trip runner families are `kafka`, `jms`, `ems` and `amqp`. Connections use MINA's existing connection configuration keys. JMS/EMS also need a compatible Java runtime, compiled bridge and the provider's permitted client libraries. The scripts require the backend environment and test-only `psutil`; Direct Kafka also needs `aiokafka`. Use deployment secret practices for real authentication values. The sample above is structural, not a usable connection.

Set-Location <checkout>
python scripts/live-messaging-soak.py --config <private-qa-config.json> --output <private-report.json> --private-diagnostics <private-log-directory>
For mode verification, supply exactly four separate fresh destinations per family, in Run/Debug/Direct/Engine order:
python scripts/live-messaging-verify.py --config <private-mode-config.json> --output <private-mode-report.json> --private-diagnostics <private-log-directory>

Public reports omit connections, credentials, payloads and provider exception text. Optional private diagnostics contain provider/runtime details and must remain protected. Resolve credentials locally; do not send passwords or tokens in chat.
Sustained generated-archive execution

`scripts/live-messaging-archive-soak.py` builds each selected format into a private ZIP, imports it in a separate Python process per worker, and repeatedly calls its generated task in one event loop. Kafka, JMS and AMQP use real network connections. Each child closes its SDK clients and Java sender workers before exiting; an unclosed-resource diagnostic or forced shutdown fails qualification.

The generated process reports its own PID so resource samples refer to the actual interpreter. On this Windows virtual environment the launcher PID returned by `Popen` is a different, small process. Earlier launcher-only measurements were explicitly invalidated and retained as `live-messaging-archive-*-launcher-measurement-2026-11-15.json`; they cannot establish application memory stability. Final reports must show `actualInterpreterIdentified: true` for every worker.

Give each format its own fresh destinations. The final local archive runs use one worker per family, 60 seconds of warmup and 900 measured seconds per format, with the same one-second minimum cycle interval. In addition to controller metrics, each generated Python process has separate gates: at most 64 MiB RSS growth, 16 extra handles, 4 extra threads and 0.5 MiB/minute late RSS slope. These gates cover the generated Python processes; nested Java process trends remain a separate measurement/qualification concern.

python scripts/live-messaging-archive-soak.py --mode python-direct --config <private-direct-config.json> --output <private-direct-report.json>
python scripts/live-messaging-archive-soak.py --mode python-engine --config <private-engine-config.json> --output <private-engine-report.json>

The final local results are `docs/validation/live-messaging-archive-direct-2026-11-15.json` and `docs/validation/live-messaging-archive-engine-2026-11-15.json`. A failed child resource gate means that archive run failed even if individual message round trips succeeded. A separate Direct startup failure on the fresh broker is retained in `live-messaging-archive-direct-second-pass-2026-11-14.json`; its original child traceback was not retained, so its cause is unresolved. Subsequent runs retain private diagnostics. Do not treat a later pass as explaining that earlier failure.
Repeated automated Debug sessions

`scripts/live-messaging-debug-soak.py` uses the same real-broker flows through `DebugManager.start`, resume and stop, repeatedly creating and closing sessions. The final local Debug run uses one worker per family, 60 seconds of warmup and 600 measured seconds, with a one-second minimum cycle interval. Its result is `docs/validation/live-messaging-debug-2026-11-15.json`. This exercises the Debug service and its session cleanup, not an interactive installed Studio GUI.

The initial Debug harness omitted Studio Stop's scoped native-process termination. That harness omission retained sender workers until cache/idle cleanup; it was corrected before the final November 15 attempt. It is not evidence that Studio's Stop endpoint omitted that cleanup.
Additional live protocol cases

The opt-in `backend/tests/test_live_messaging_services.py` checks default AMQP expiry/auto-settlement, positive expiry in milliseconds, custom properties/content type/priority/correlation, manual settlement, actual message expiry, and JMS request/reply through a temporary reply destination with correlation preserved. The local run passed all four tests against Artemis. These are separate protocol checks, not additional cloud or EMS evidence.

To run them, set `MINA_LIVE_EDGE_CONFIG` to a protected JSON file containing `approvedTestDestinations: true`, `amqpConnection`, three dedicated existing `amqpQueues`, `jmsConnection`, and a dedicated `requestReplyQueue`, then run `python -m unittest tests.test_live_messaging_services -v` from `backend`. With no explicit configuration, discovery skips these live checks. Do not point them at business queues.
python scripts/live-messaging-debug-soak.py --config <private-debug-config.json> --output <private-debug-report.json> --private-diagnostics <private-log-directory>
Services still needing live qualification

rows: Approved QA project, publisher/subscriber credentials or ADC setup, dedicated topic/subscription, IAM permissions and certificate requirements
Approved server, provider Java client JARs, credentials, dedicated queues/topics and acknowledgement/transaction requirements
Approved QA system, permitted JCo JAR/native library, credentials, allowed test RFC such as an approved connection-test function, and declared listener/IDoc test scope

blocks.text: The existing `scripts/sap-production-soak.py` accepts a protected configuration based on `docs/sap-soak-config.example.json`. Do not run posting, update, IDoc or failure-injection cases without the corresponding QA scope. Its percentile fields describe the retained window; total counts and min/mean/max describe the whole run.
Until those inputs are supplied, these services are **not live-verified**. Unit doubles, an emulator or an alternative JMS provider must not be reported as a cloud, EMS or SAP pass.
Activity resource verification

This review extends the File/FTP/SFTP and HTTP/database checks to the remaining activity families. It checks resource ownership, failure cleanup, bounded caches, concurrency and generated Python behavior. Passing local checks does not establish production readiness for every external provider or workload.
Fixes

Pub/Sub service-account refresh closes its temporary Requests session on success and failure. Runtime publisher shutdown closes the transport even if publisher stop fails; a JMS shutdown failure does not skip other owned clients.
Kafka transaction locks use at most 64 stripes rather than retaining every dynamic configuration fingerprint.

AMQP receive and connection-test resources close on empty results, automatic acknowledgement, setup errors, receive errors and settlement errors. Manual acknowledgement transfers ownership to the returned settlement callback. Azure identity credentials created by MINA close with their client, including constructor failures. These changes are shared by generated Direct and Engine AMQP adapters.

Direct Excel closes its read-only workbook in a finally block. The default start-row calculation no longer refers to an uninitialized header-row variable. Run, Debug and both generated archive entry points are covered with a real XLSX file.
Java invocation waits for the killed process to exit on timeout before deleting its temporary compilation directory.
Direct Pub/Sub pull closes its subscriber transport on success and failure.

Direct Kafka and Pub/Sub retain at most 32 publisher clients each. Additional configurations use one-shot clients and close them after use. Overflow Pub/Sub publishes wait for provider confirmation before releasing the transport, even when the normal mode is buffered. Kafka startup failure or cancellation stops the partially initialized producer. Direct Kafka initialization locks use at most 64 stripes per event loop; application shutdown clears the registry. Cache keys contain hashes instead of serialized credentials.
Coverage and limits

rows: Mapper, transforms, scripted Transform and six XML/JSON/data format activities
Full backend regressions, Run/Debug/archive parity cases, concurrent local soak
Representative customer schema sizes and sustained deployment workloads
Tasks, subtasks, groups, forks/joins, faults, mapping deletion and basic activities
Full backend suite, including 100-branch join and generated execution tests
Real XLSX Run/Debug/archive regression, Java process timeout cleanup, Python/Excel local soak
User-supplied code behavior and large workbooks
Publisher reuse, failure injection, bounded dynamic-configuration checks and generated adapter tests
Live broker/cloud soak, TLS/SASL/IAM, ordering, redelivery and failover
Existing memory-mode/bridge regressions and adapter ownership tests with doubles
Live broker/provider libraries, settlement, transaction and failover qualification
Existing parser, listener/session and generated-adapter regressions
Licensed live SAP connectivity, native-library memory and reconnect soak
Complete backend regressions plus the earlier live local HTTP/HTTPS sustained verification
Remote provider and deployed ingress configuration
Earlier live local connector soaks plus full regression suite
Database vendors and remote servers unavailable in this environment
Deployment scheduler behavior, retention sizing and recovery after infrastructure loss

blocks.text: The Studio checks are automated designer/Help tests and backend execution paths. An interactive installed-app session and a fresh Windows installer are not part of this verification.

Python Invoke executes user code in a thread. Its timeout stops awaiting the result; Python cannot forcibly stop arbitrary code already running in that thread. Use a separately supervised worker for untrusted or potentially nonterminating code. This review does not claim that changing garbage-collector settings makes such code safe.

Mapping, parsing and Excel results are materialized in memory. Their memory requirement scales with payload/result size; this check uses bounded representative payloads and does not establish constant-memory processing for arbitrarily large documents. Buffered publisher delivery and unconfirmed manual acknowledgements must also be sized and monitored for the deployment.
Reproducible checks
Use the backend environment with its optional connector dependencies and test-only psutil/openpyxl. No customer credentials are needed for the new resource tests.

Set-Location <checkout>\backend
python -m unittest tests.test_remaining_activity_resources tests.test_publisher_reuse tests.test_raw_python tests.test_engine_export -v
Set-Location ..
python scripts/activity-resource-soak.py --seconds 600 --warmup 30 --output tmp/activity-resource-soak.json
Set-Location frontend
node --test tests/*.test.mjs
node --test scripts/documentation.test.mjs
npm.cmd run build

The eight-worker soak concurrently exercises Mapper and scripted Transform, six format operations, source and Direct Excel, and source and Direct Python invocation. It records actual operation counts, errors, RSS, traced Python heap, OS handles and threads. It does not force garbage collection. Gates are at most 64 MiB RSS growth, 8 MiB Python heap growth, 8 additional handles, 2 additional threads, and a late RSS slope at most 0.5 MiB/minute. Sampling starts after warmup. A ten-minute local check is not a long-duration remote-provider soak.
Measured results are stored in `docs/validation/remaining-activities-soak-2026-11-14.json`. The final regression summary and changed-file list are in `docs/REMAINING_ACTIVITY_CHANGED_FILES.md`.
HTTP and database memory/concurrency verification

The 30-minute HTTP/database soak **passed both client and listener resource gates**: **131,385 measured operations**, zero unexpected operation errors, and 2,348 intentional response-limit failures followed by successful requests. These negative checks are expected; they are not hidden unexpected failures.
Confirmed fixes
HTTP per-destination permits previously retained a semaphore for every contacted

destination. They now retain active requests and waiters only, removing an idle route without creating a second gate while another request still waits. A 5,000-destination regression leaves no idle route history. Timeout and policy failures release references too.
Scoped HTTP cleanup attempts all client closes and removes owned token entries
even if one close fails, while preserving other scopes and reporting the first close failure. Shared clients still have their existing quota and connection limits.
Reset/aborted HTTP connections now cancel keepalive timers unconditionally.
The HTTP/1 status-line application wrapper no longer captures its owning
protocol, releasing closed connections without waiting for cyclic GC.
HTTP listener setup now releases warmed executors if TLS/configuration setup or
worker warm-up fails. Warm-up failure aborts its barrier so waiting workers can exit.
JSON schema validation now reuses a bounded set of draft-specific validator

types. Each call still gets a fresh schema-bound instance, offline registry and isolated ContextVar budget; schemas and input values are not cached. This removes per-validation class creation and reduces collectable metadata/GC pressure.
JDBC metadata browsing closes table and column cursors explicitly, including
exceptions, before closing the owned session. Snowflake connection tests, metadata and operations likewise close their cursors and connections.
Automatically generated Snowflake CSV files close and delete on writer, PUT,
COPY/load and normal completion paths. User-supplied files are preserved.
Direct JDBC archives now include the Snowflake helper even without a separate

Snowflake activity. Both archive formats declare native driver prerequisites and Java/JDBC prerequisites from the configured mode. Driver/mode property choices are resolved together per environment, avoiding false native Oracle requirements created by mixing separate profiles. Native-only flows retain their existing behavior without a Java prerequisite.
The final activity implementations were unchanged throughout this reported soak. Exporter fixes also passed separate archive tests. No dependency versions changed.
Listener reference cycle and first-pass findings

The first 30-minute pass met client gates but showed listener RSS rising as high as 243.3 MiB before falling back near its starting level. Inspection found `protocol.app -> closure -> protocol` in MINA's status-line wrapper. Capturing only the h11 connection removes that cycle. An additional inherited reset path left a keepalive callback retaining a closed protocol. MINA now always cancels that timer on disconnect, including errors. Its GC-disabled regression failed before the fix and passed afterward. A regression with cyclic GC disabled failed before the fix and passed afterward: the protocol now releases through reference counting. A second pressure source was per-call validator class creation. Draft-specific bounded type reuse removes that churn, retaining per-call schemas and budgets. No forced server GC or global GC tuning was added.

A fresh full 30-minute pass below uses the final wrapper and adds separate listener resource gates. Its listener peak RSS was 68.7 MiB; idle RSS changed -4.94 MiB, handles +3, and threads +0. The first-pass samples are preserved in `docs/validation/http-database-first-pass-2026-11-13.json`.
Sustained workload and environment

Tested on Windows-10-10.0.26200-SP0, Python 3.11.9, HTTPX 0.28.1, HTTPcore 1.0.9 and cryptography 46.0.0. The production MINA listener implementation hosted separate HTTP and verified-TLS HTTPS endpoints in another process. Outbound HTTP Request and OpenAPI-based REST Invoke echoed and checked 64 KiB JSON payloads. SQLite WAL and a fresh disposable TLS MySQL instance performed bound INSERT/SELECT/DELETE cycles and checked values. No existing database or customer endpoint was used.

Warm-up was 120 seconds, followed by **1,800 measured seconds with 20 concurrent workers**. The longer warm-up covers HTTP/TLS/parser setup and client-pool startup. Every 25th HTTP/HTTPS/REST cycle first triggers a small response-byte limit, checks its fault, then performs a normal successful request.

Client gates were unchanged: zero unexpected errors; at most 64 MiB RSS growth, 8 MiB retained Python growth, 0.5 MiB/min late RSS slope, 20 additional quiescent handles and 4 additional quiescent threads. Warmed idle-to-idle measurements and periodic forced GC normalize samples. Production activities do not force GC after each operation. Listener-process RSS, threads and handles are recorded separately; the same RSS/slope/handle/thread bounds now gate that process too. Test processes and disposable services are shut down after the run.

Cycle latency includes tracing, complete request/response/schema work and three statements for a database cycle. It is not a per-statement throughput guarantee or a controlled comparison against the earlier File/SFTP workload.
Short-lived native thread checks

Separate real-service probes each created 2,600 fresh threads: verified HTTPS with connection reuse disabled, and a new verified-TLS MySQL connection issuing SELECT 1. Samples below compare post-warm-up active states. The probes then close their owned clients. They did not reproduce the SFTP-style per-thread growth.

This does not repair the upstream cryptography raw-thread control documented in the SFTP investigation, nor certify arbitrary native extensions or caller-created cryptographic threads. It checks these actual HTTP/TLS and MySQL paths.
Execution and archive checks
The final backend suite ran 231 tests: **230 passed**, with the live
PostgreSQL test explicitly skipped because no disposable DSN was configured.
After the protocol fix, all **70 HTTP/resource tests** passed, including
actual status-line/hosted API and archive regressions.
The final suite includes **58 archive/resource tests**, including **17 focused

resource/schema cases**. These include shared-gate concurrency, startup failure, CSV cleanup, preservation of user files, driver-mode preflight and executing the Snowflake JDBC helper in fresh Direct and Engine archive processes with an injected driver. Injected Snowflake checks are not live cloud qualification.
Real HTTP/HTTPS, HTTP/REST response handling, SQLite and MySQL checks exercise

Run, Debug, Direct Python, Engine Python and Direct zip execution. HTTP/2, HTTP/3, SSE/WebSocket and authentication policies have functional regressions in the suite; they are not the sustained profile above.
All **150 frontend component tests** passed. Interactive GUI and a fresh
Windows installer build were not part of this backend/resource change.

Oracle, SQL Server, PostgreSQL, DB2, Snowflake, Databricks and MariaDB were not qualified against live providers here. Driver/adaptor and compiled Java bridge regressions cannot substitute for their real authentication, procedures, paging, failover and long-duration workloads. External OAuth/LDAP/proxy/Redis services also require deployment-specific sustained qualification. Thirty local minutes do not establish multi-day production behavior.
Reproduce and operational limits

Use a source checkout and an isolated test Python with the backend dependencies, psutil, cryptography and (for MySQL) PyMySQL. Set `MINA_TEST_MYSQLD` to an installed mysqld executable to enable a fresh loopback datadir; otherwise that lane is omitted. Run from the repository root:
python scripts/http-database-soak.py --duration-seconds 1800 --warmup-seconds 120 --report tmp/http-db-soak.json
The harness returns nonzero if a client resource gate fails. Source fingerprints, resource samples and native probe measurements are in `docs/validation/http-database-memory-2026-11-13.json`.

Limits apply per request/query, not to the entire process. Large decoded objects, Debug snapshots and concurrent result sets multiply peak memory. Set sensible maximum rows/subset sizes, body limits and connection/thread limits; use file streaming when the response contract allows it. Native TLS connections did not need the SFTP-specific transport-worker workaround in these tests.
See [HTTP capabilities](HTTP_REST_CAPABILITIES.md), [connector readiness](FILE_TRANSFER_DATABASE_READINESS.md) and [Python archive modes](PYTHON_EXPORT.md).

pages.title: Windows SFTP native memory fix and verification

blocks.text: Windows SFTP native memory fix and verification

The Windows SFTP connection-churn issue is mitigated in MINA by bounded, persistent SSH transport workers. The fresh 30-minute, 22-worker soak **passed all original gates**, completing **217,489 measured operations with zero errors**. The upstream raw-thread behavior still reproduces; the MINA SFTP path avoids it.
Implementation and compatibility

Previously each SSH transport created a new thread. A network-free X25519 control reproduced native memory growth on Windows despite stable Python allocations and handles. Replacing cryptography with two newer versions did not fix that pattern.

MINA now supplies a transport class through Paramiko's documented [transport_factory extension point](https://docs.paramiko.org/en/3.5/api/client.html#paramiko.client.SSHClient.connect). The class runs the normal SSH protocol loop on a bounded set of lazy daemon workers. Its start, completion and join behavior follows each individual transport. Workers survive between connections; completed targets are cleared so they do not retain transports, credentials, keys or payloads. Unexpected job termination releases capacity without killing the persistent worker.

Each activity still opens, authenticates and closes a **fresh connection**. Host-key verification, authentication methods, key exchange/cipher choices, configured socket waits and the subsystem handshake deadline are preserved. There is no authenticated connection cache, global OpenSSL cleanup, working-set trimming, forced per-operation GC or native-symbol patch. Linux and macOS retain their normal transport path. No runtime dependency versions were changed.

`MINA_SFTP_TRANSPORT_WORKERS` defaults to **32**, accepts **1–128**, and is read when the Windows transport factory is first created. Set it before the first connection and restart the runtime to change it. At capacity, an incoming connection waits up to its configured timeout, then fails without closing other sessions. An invalid setting fails explicitly. Persistent idle worker threads are intentional and bounded; the factory is initialized once even during concurrent first connections.
The shared helper is included by the existing Direct and Engine archive module closures, so no exporter/runtime fork or deployment dependency was needed.
Sustained verification

Tested on Windows-10-10.0.26200-SP0, Python 3.11.9, Paramiko 3.5.1 and cryptography 46.0.0. Servers ran in a separate disposable loopback process. MySQL used a fresh datadir and verified TLS; SQLite used WAL. FTP/FTPS and SFTP used real protocol servers, with verified FTPS certificates and SFTP host keys. No customer services were used.
Warm-up: 60 seconds. Measured duration: 1,800 seconds. Payload: 64 KiB. Gates and 22-worker counts were unchanged from the failed baseline.

The gates remain: zero operation errors; at most 64 MiB RSS growth, 8 MiB retained Python allocations, 0.5 MiB/min late RSS slope, 20 quiescent handles and 4 quiescent threads of growth. Measurements normalize GC and compare warmed idle states. Instrumented cycle p95 includes multi-operation cycles and tracing; it is not a throughput promise. The baseline and follow-up had different background test loads, so latency differences are not a controlled benchmark.

An additional **10-minute untraced real-SFTP** diagnostic used two concurrent workers against the disposable server and completed 5,521 upload/download/delete cycles without errors. Its late RSS slope was 0.110 MiB/min. This supports stability outside tracemalloc. Server metrics are separate: the raw Paramiko test-server fixture is not MINA's SFTP client and still uses the upstream thread-per-connection server path.
Native controls and functional coverage

Each cryptography version was tested in fresh control processes: empty threads, same-thread crypto, raw new-thread crypto and the MINA bounded-worker path. Each case warms 500 iterations and measures 4,000. The raw failure remains visible; `--managed` gates the mitigated path against the controls.
All **252 main backend tests** passed, including real FTP/FTPS/SFTP transfers,
Run, Debug, Direct Python, Engine Python and Direct Python zip execution; HTTP, database and compiled Java JDBC bridge regressions also passed.
All **7 focused SFTP tests** passed: bounded capacity and recovery after failure,

concurrent factory lookup, closed-transport collection, capacity timeout without disturbing a live connection, invalid settings, encrypted RSA key authentication, incorrect-passphrase rejection, and parallel 2 MiB streamed payloads on distinct SSH servers with host-key isolation. Key-auth checks also execute in Run, Debug and both archive formats.
Separate tests with **Paramiko 5.1.0** passed (7 network/lifecycle checks,
6 key-auth/lifecycle checks, and the added multi-server streaming check). These used an isolated test directory; MINA's pinned package was not replaced.
All **150 frontend component tests** passed. Interactive GUI validation and a
fresh Windows installer build were not performed for this backend-only change.

A 30-minute local soak and 10-minute diagnostic do not certify every server, Windows release or multi-day workload. Validate deployment OS, keys, host trust, network failures, intended concurrency and large files on the target service. The measured activity/helper source hashes are recorded in `docs/validation/sftp-windows-memory-fixed-2026-11-13.json`.
Reproduce

Use an isolated test Python with the test dependencies described in the connector operational guide. Set `MINA_TEST_MYSQLD` to a mysqld executable to include the fresh disposable MySQL lane. From the source repository root:

python scripts/connector-soak.py --duration-seconds 1800 --warmup-seconds 60 --report tmp/sftp-fixed-soak.json
python scripts/connector-native-memory.py --managed --report tmp/sftp-fixed-native.json

The original raw-dependency diagnostic remains available by omitting `--managed`. It may fail while the bounded MINA path passes; that is why both results are recorded. See [the pre-fix baseline](CONNECTOR_SOAK_RESULTS.md), [the operational guide](FILE_TRANSFER_DATABASE_READINESS.md) and [the environment variable reference](ENVIRONMENT_VARIABLES.md).
Connector concurrency and memory verification — 2026-11-13

This is the **pre-fix baseline**. MINA's Windows SFTP implementation subsequently changed to bounded persistent transport workers. See [the follow-up fix and verification](SFTP_WINDOWS_MEMORY_FIX.md). The original failed measurements below are preserved for comparison.

The 30-minute measured workload completed with **zero operation errors**, but **failed the native-memory stability gate**. This is not a blanket production certification. At the time of this baseline, the Windows SFTP dependency finding below remained unresolved.
Environment and workload
