Windows Windows-10-10.0.26200-SP0; Python 3.11.9; Paramiko 3.5.1; cryptography 46.0.0; pyftpdlib 2.2.0; PyMySQL 1.2.4; psutil 7.2.2. 22 concurrent workers, 64 KiB payloads, 60-second warm-up followed by 1,800 measured seconds. FTP, verified FTPS and host-key-verified SFTP used disposable loopback servers in another process. SQLite used WAL; MySQL used a fresh datadir and verified TLS. No customer endpoints or databases were used.

Total measured operations: **211,389**. File cycles write/copy/read/list; transfer cycles upload/download/delete; database cycles insert/select/delete. Checksums and selected database values were verified. Each transfer operation opens and closes a connection, deliberately stressing handshake and cleanup. Latency measurements include tracing overhead and complete multi-operation cycles. The bounded latency sample retains the most recent 4,096 cycles per lane.
Memory and garbage collection
Failed gates: Late RSS slope exceeds 0.5 MiB/minute.

GC was forced only for measurement normalization. Native RSS was not trimmed. The gates are: zero errors, no more than 64 MiB RSS growth, 8 MiB retained Python allocations, 0.5 MiB/min late RSS slope, 20 quiescent handles or 4 quiescent threads of growth. An early short test exposed initialization effects; warm-up and idle-to-idle resource comparisons were added before this full run. No gate was relaxed to turn the native-memory failure into a pass.
Isolated Windows dependency finding

A network-free reproducer performs the same X25519 key generation/exchange on one thread or newly created/joined threads, with empty threads as a control. Each case runs in a fresh process, warms 500 iterations, then measures 4,000.

Handles did not accumulate, and retained Python allocations were about 2 KiB per case. A separate untraced SFTP test showed continuing RSS growth; removing the subsystem handshake timer or selecting Python's malloc allocator did not remove it. FTPS and MySQL isolation checks stabilized after initialization. These results isolate a native allocation problem in the Windows cryptographic thread path; they do not identify a particular C allocation or prove behavior on Linux.

The compatible patch and current cryptography releases were tested in temporary directories only. Neither fixed the finding, so runtime dependency requirements were not changed. No global OpenSSL cleanup, private native-symbol patch, working-set trimming or security downgrade was introduced. OpenSSL documents platform-dependent thread cleanup for static linking; this is relevant context, not proof of the precise cause: [OpenSSL initialization and thread cleanup](https://docs.openssl.org/master/man3/OPENSSL_init_crypto/).

This baseline did not qualify high-churn, long-lived Windows SFTP workloads. A fix or bounded integration mitigation must pass the controls and a fresh soak. A multi-hour/overnight run on the deployment OS and real target servers is still required for release qualification. A 30-minute local run does not certify all server products or deployment durations.
Product fixes and regression coverage
Native JDBC connections shared by parallel transaction branches now serialize

statement execution/fetching, commit, rollback and close using a lock owned by the session. Independent connections remain parallel. A real TLS MySQL test runs 24 concurrent inserts through eight workers sharing one session.
SQLite and real MySQL failure tests check closed sessions/sockets while exception
tracebacks remain retained, then verify session objects collect after releasing those tracebacks. No global connection or lock cache was introduced.
The HTTP failure came from CONNECT in generated ordinary receiver defaults.

AI receiver defaults now exclude it; listener configuration rejects unsupported methods explicitly. Studio displays legacy unsupported selections and provides a repair action that retains supported methods. Ordinary application methods remain tested; CONNECT tunnel handling is not implemented as a fake API reply.

The main backend suite passed 245 tests. An additional 26-test suite passed with one live PostgreSQL test skipped because no disposable PostgreSQL DSN was supplied (25 executed successfully), including real Java bridge compilation. A 10-test GC and concurrency recheck passed. All 150 frontend tests passed, including method repair. Run and Debug, Direct Python, Engine Python and Direct Python zip paths were exercised by integration tests with real loopback FTP/FTPS/SFTP and MySQL. Studio verification used automated component and API tests; this run did not complete an interactive GUI verification.
Oracle, SQL Server, DB2, MariaDB, Snowflake and Databricks were not qualified against live servers here. Adapter regressions cannot replace that qualification.
Reproduce

From the repository root, use an isolated test Python with psutil, pyftpdlib, pyOpenSSL, Paramiko, cryptography and PyMySQL available. Set `MINA_TEST_MYSQLD` to an installed mysqld executable to include the disposable MySQL lane.

python scripts/connector-soak.py --duration-seconds 1800 --warmup-seconds 60 --report tmp/connector-soak-report.json
python scripts/connector-native-memory.py --report tmp/connector-native-memory.json

Both tools return a nonzero exit code when a resource gate fails. See the machine-readable measurements in `docs/validation/connector-soak-2026-11-13.json` and [the operational guide](FILE_TRANSFER_DATABASE_READINESS.md). The recorded source hashes identify the workload version measured; a later harness-only change creates the tmp directory when a custom report path is used. Activity implementations were unchanged throughout the measured run.

pages.title: File transfers, database operations, and Input XPath

blocks.text: File transfers, database operations, and Input XPath
XPath in every activity Input editor

Open **Input → Functions → XPath functions** for any activity, including File, FTP, SFTP, JDBC, Call Sub Task, and End. Choose XPath 1.0 or 2.0, select a function, enter XPath arguments, and drag the prepared expression to a field. The catalog includes descriptions and overloads and works before runtime loads.

Type a function prefix such as `flo`, `token`, or `xs:da` for suggestions. Use arrow keys and Tab or Enter to select one; functions that need arguments retain focus inside the inserted call. Namespace prefixes are included in completion. Data references and quoted constants remain distinct from XPath.

Use `xpath1("expression")` or `xpath2("expression")`; unversioned `xpath` in general activity inputs uses XPath 1.0. The source defaults to the previous activity output: XML text or an object containing `xmlString`, `xml`, `content`, or `body`. To select another source explicitly:

xpath2("sum(/orders/order/@amount)", ${input.xmlString})
xpath2("tokenize('a,b,c', ',')")
xpath1("local-name(/*)")
Without an XML payload, context-free functions run against an empty `<input/>` context. Supply explicit XML for path-based expressions; an explicit invalid XML source raises an error.

Declare namespace prefixes in the XML document for namespace-qualified paths. Mapper's additional XML binding configuration remains available for Mapper. XPath sequences become lists; exact decimal results may be strings to retain precision. Existing restrictions on XML size, external documents, DTDs and regex execution apply to activity Inputs. Run, Debug and both Python formats use these evaluators; exports include XML requirements when any activity uses XPath.
Local File activities

Read, Write, List, Poll, Copy, Rename and Delete share an implementation in Studio and both Python formats. File I/O runs off the Studio runtime event loop. Paths must be nonempty; an empty path never selects the working directory. Copy and Rename require a destination, reject the same file (including hard links), reject overlapping directory trees, and check source existence before replacing a destination.

Non-append Write and file Copy stage complete content in the destination directory before publishing it. Overwrite uses filesystem replacement; exclusive creation uses a hard link to avoid clobbering a concurrent writer. The destination filesystem must support this operation; unsupported filesystems fail rather than silently overwriting data. Rename no longer deletes the old destination first. A failed publication preserves the existing destination and removes the temporary file. Append retains normal append semantics and is not transactional.

Directory Copy completes a staged tree before replacing the destination. Directory replacement retains the old tree as `.mina-backup-*` during publication and restores it if publication fails. A process or machine crash between the two renames can leave a backup that must be recovered manually. Failed backup cleanup returns `backupPath` and `cleanupWarning`; do not delete a retained backup before checking the published tree. Avoid competing writers to the same directory. These are filesystem safeguards, not distributed transactions or a power-loss durability guarantee.

Read supports GZIP with the same Compression selection used for Write. Its **Maximum decompressed read bytes** Input applies while streaming decompression, preventing an oversized compressed payload from being expanded entirely first. Zero is unlimited. Select the correct encoding or Binary mode. Deleting a symbolic link removes the link itself; filesystem-root deletion is rejected.
FTP, FTPS and SFTP

Use an FTP shared connection for FTP/FTPS and an SFTP shared connection for SSH transfers. Get, Put, Directory, Change Directory and Delete support dynamic paths. Binary Put accepts base64 text or bytes; Get returns `contentBase64` and `size`. Select Binary for arbitrary binary payloads.

FTP connection options include Passive mode, Timeout, Use verified TLS (FTPS), Implicit TLS, a trusted CA bundle/directory, and optional client certificate/key files. FTPS verifies server identity, requires TLS 1.2 or later, and protects both control and data channels. Explicit TLS normally uses port 21; implicit uses 990. Plain FTP remains available but does not encrypt credentials or file data. CA directories use the OpenSSL hashed-directory layout; use a CA bundle file for an ordinary PEM bundle.

SFTP rejects unknown host keys by default. Supply a Known hosts file and password or private-key authentication. Timeouts cover connection, banner, authentication, channel opening and transfer I/O. Disabling host verification accepts an unverified server identity.

Get exposes **Maximum download bytes** in Input: zero leaves downloads unlimited; a positive integer stops a transfer that exceeds the limit. Set **Download directly to local file** (`localPath`) to stream without assembling the payload in memory. The file is staged locally and published only after a successful transfer; a size limit or network failure preserves an existing destination. Set Overwrite and Create directories explicitly. File mode returns `localPath` and `size`, with null `content`/`contentBase64`. Without `localPath`, the activity returns in-memory data.

Put can stream a **Local file to upload** instead of inline content. **Publish upload by remote rename** (`atomicUpload`) writes a unique sibling temporary file before renaming it to the requested name. Failures attempt to remove that temporary file. FTP rename overwrite semantics depend on the server. SFTP replacement with Overwrite requires the server's POSIX rename extension; it fails without deleting the destination when unsupported. A killed process or broken connection can leave a `.mina-*.tmp` remote file for later cleanup. Remote publication does not guarantee disk durability or exactly-once delivery. Design retries around idempotent names and business acknowledgements.
Invalid operations, missing paths and remote-path control characters fail before connecting. Connections close on authentication, transfer and cleanup failures.
Database activities

Query, Insert, Update, Delete, Dynamic/Direct SQL, Truncate and Stored Procedure operations depend on the selected driver's support. Use bound parameters for values; do not concatenate untrusted data into SQL. Prepared parameter types are applied before execution. Integer parameters reject fractional/nonfinite values; Boolean parameters reject unrecognized text. Positional parameters and positional batch records use the declared types as well as named parameter records. Declared decimal values retain decimal precision in native Oracle, SQL Server, MySQL/MariaDB and Java JDBC bindings rather than passing through a binary float.

Batch writes roll back on error when the activity owns the transaction. A JDBC Transaction group owns commit/rollback for its member operations. Paging, row limits, INSERT RETURNING, empty-string handling, update-with-insert fallback, and procedures depend on the provider. Boolean options supplied as `"false"` are disabled. SQLite per-activity busy timeouts are restored on shared connections. Oracle native call timeouts and SQL Server ODBC query timeouts are applied and restored per activity. MySQL/MariaDB shared connections expose socket Read and Write timeouts, defaulting to the connection timeout when blank; these are socket wait bounds, not a server-side statement cancellation guarantee. Providing a MySQL/MariaDB CA certificate enables certificate and hostname verification.

Stored Procedure configuration includes **Add procedure parameter**, datatype and IN/OUT/INOUT direction. OUT-only parameters are excluded from required Input fields and appear as typed `outParameters.<name>` outputs. MySQL/MariaDB retrieves OUT values from the server after draining procedure results; native Oracle uses typed driver variables; Oracle/SQL Server JDBC uses CallableStatement and registered OUT parameters. PostgreSQL CALL returns its output row. Procedure names must be qualified identifiers rather than SQL fragments. Parameter names must be unique identifiers. Overriding transaction behavior requires a JDBC Transaction group; standalone activities cannot report success while closing an uncommitted private transaction.

Connection probes use Oracle DUAL, DB2 VALUES, or SELECT 1 as appropriate. MySQL/MariaDB metadata uses the selected database. Configure supported driver versions, timeouts, verified TLS, least-privilege credentials and server-side access rules. External driver JARs and certificates remain deployment inputs.
Verification scope
Memory and cancellation controls

File Read returns content in memory; set `maxReadBytes` or use Exclude file content for metadata-only reads. In-memory FTP/SFTP Get also needs `maxDownloadBytes`. For large transfers, set `localPath` so Get/Put streams through a local file. Base64 output and decoded text require additional allocations when returned in memory. Inline File Write/Put content is already part of the process payload; use local-file streaming or File Copy for large file-to-file work.

File List/Poll and FTP/SFTP Directory accept `maxEntries`. A positive limit fails the operation when exceeded, rather than silently truncating a polling snapshot. Zero preserves unlimited legacy behavior. Simple filename patterns stream local directory scanning; complex path-glob patterns use the platform glob implementation and can allocate additional scan buffers. Recursive scans do not follow symbolic links or Windows directory reparse points in the streaming path. Files that disappear during a local listing are skipped.

Stop/Cancel signals background I/O at chunk and publication checkpoints in Studio and both Python formats. A cancelled staged copy/download is not published and its temporary file is removed. A blocked socket can still take up to its socket timeout to return to a checkpoint. SFTP subsystem negotiation also has an explicit deadline. Cancellation cannot undo an already completed rename/delete, an append, or bytes already written by a non-atomic remote upload; filesystem primitives already executing cannot be forcibly interrupted safely.

Owned read/transfer buffers and network/file handles are closed on success and failure, including when exception tracebacks remain retained for debugging. Automated checks cover a 32 MiB streamed download with under 2 MiB of tracked Python allocations, repeated reads without retained payload growth, failure-buffer closure, cancellation cleanup in portable archives, listing limits and a stalled SFTP subsystem. These are bounded regression checks, not a whole-process RSS, native-library leak or deployment-duration soak certification. Process inputs, outputs and debug history intentionally retain data while their execution records remain available. Configure concurrency and retention for the intended workload.

Completed/failed/stopped debug-session history is bounded to eight sessions by default (`MINA_DEBUG_HISTORY_LIMIT`). Debug log buffers default to 10,000 entries (`MINA_DEBUG_LOG_LIMIT`) and drop the oldest entries while recording `logEntriesDropped` in the debug API. Set positive integer environment values on the Studio backend to change these limits. Active sessions are never evicted by the completed-session limit; stop sessions that are no longer needed. Count limits are not byte quotas: large payloads still need the file/transfer limits above.

Automated tests exercise local files, actual loopback FTP/FTPS/SFTP transfers, binary data, host-key rejection, failure cleanup, download limits, generic Input XPath, SQLite CRUD/batch rollback and database adapter/probe behavior. Integration tests cover Run, Debug, Direct Python, Engine Python and Direct Python zip execution. Tests inject replacement failures and concurrent destination creation, enforce decompression/download limits, verify trusted and untrusted FTPS certificates, and compile the real Java bridge for CallableStatement behavior. Studio component tests cover dynamic transfer/read controls, procedure editing, duplicate-name warnings and typed OUT fields.

The opt-in MySQL fixture starts a new loopback-only server with a private datadir and generated CA/server certificates. It checks real CRUD, positional batch coercion and rollback, paging, procedures with OUT values, socket timeout and transaction-group rollback, including Run, Debug and both Python formats. Existing MySQL installations and their data are never used by this fixture.

These tests do not certify every production server, database release or network. The PostgreSQL sample suite requires `MINA_TEST_POSTGRES_DSN` for a disposable database and explicitly skips live tests when absent. Oracle, SQL Server, DB2, MariaDB, Snowflake and Databricks require live services, drivers and credentials to qualify production interoperability. Test TLS chains, procedures/OUT parameters, isolation, large transfers, failure recovery and concurrency on the target systems.

Native JDBC sessions shared by parallel branches in one transaction serialize statement execution, result fetching, commit, rollback and close on that session. DB-API connections must not receive overlapping protocol requests. Separate connections remain independent; use batches or a transaction group when reducing connection handshakes matters. The session owns its lock, with no global registry retaining closed sessions. Failure cleanup tests retain exception tracebacks to check that sockets close before those tracebacks are released, then check that session objects can be garbage collected.

JDBC metadata browsing explicitly closes the table and column cursors before closing its connection, including failed browse requests. Snowflake query, metadata and connection-test paths close their cursors as well as connections. Automatically generated bulk-load CSV files are closed and removed after success, writer failures and upload/load failures. A user-supplied `filePath` remains owned by the user and is never removed by that cleanup.

The follow-up [HTTP/database resource verification](HTTP_DATABASE_MEMORY_VERIFICATION.md) covers sustained SQLite and verified-TLS MySQL traffic, HTTP/HTTPS listeners and outbound HTTP/REST calls. Other vendor adapters require their own live qualification.
Concurrent and sustained resource checks

Run `scripts/connector-soak.py` from a source checkout with test-only `psutil`, `pyftpdlib`, `pyOpenSSL`, Paramiko and PyMySQL available in the test Python environment. These test tools are not added to shipped runtime requirements. The optional `MINA_TEST_MYSQLD` executable enables a fresh loopback TLS MySQL instance with a disposable datadir. The harness does not use existing databases.
python scripts/connector-soak.py --duration-seconds 1800 --warmup-seconds 60 --report tmp/connector-soak-report.json

The workload uses 22 workers when MySQL is enabled: File 4, FTP 4, FTPS 2, SFTP 4, SQLite 4 and MySQL 4. Transfers use 64 KiB payloads and verify checksums; database cycles bind parameters and verify retrieved values. Servers run in a separate process. Metrics include client/server RSS, client handles and threads, tracked Python allocations, GC collection counts, uncollectable counts and cycle latencies. Instrumented latencies include complete cycles and profiling overhead; they are not single-operation throughput guarantees.

Warm-up and quiescent before/after measurements separate native library initialization from retained handles. The harness checks operation errors, retained Python allocations, RSS growth and its late-run slope, handles and threads. Forced GC is used for measurement normalization; production activities do not force a collection after every operation. RSS includes native libraries, allocator caches and profiling overhead, so a flat Python heap alone cannot establish that native memory is stable. See the recorded soak results for the tested environment and any resource-growth findings and follow-up verification.

On Windows, SFTP uses a bounded set of persistent daemon transport workers through Paramiko's `transport_factory`. A new authenticated SSH connection is still opened and closed for every operation. Workers retain no completed connection/job target, payload or credentials. This bounds the native per-thread cryptography state that grew when every transport created a new thread. Host-key checks, algorithms, authentication, socket waits and subsystem negotiation timeouts remain enabled. Linux/macOS continue using the normal Paramiko transport implementation.

`MINA_SFTP_TRANSPORT_WORKERS` defaults to 32 and accepts 1–128. Workers start lazily and remain idle between jobs; their count is intentionally bounded, rather than returning to zero after every transfer. Once all are occupied, a new connection waits up to its configured timeout, then raises an SFTP capacity timeout. It does not close another connection to make room. Choose a limit appropriate to the deployment's simultaneous transfers and set it before the first connection; restart to change it. An invalid value is a configuration error, with no silent fallback to unbounded threads. See the Windows SFTP memory verification report.
To isolate cryptography allocations from SSH, networking and MINA, run:
python scripts/connector-native-memory.py --managed --report tmp/connector-native-memory.json

This uses fresh processes for empty threads, cryptographic work on one thread, the same work on newly created/joined threads, and MINA's bounded worker path. With `--managed`, the gate applies to the bounded worker result and the raw upstream result remains in the report. Without it, the gate still diagnoses the upstream new-thread behavior, which MINA's Windows SFTP path now avoids. It records RSS, Python allocations, handles and GC information after warm-up. A failed native growth gate remains a release-qualification failure even if functional tests pass. Do not call global OpenSSL cleanup or trim the process working set to hide growth; neither is a safe per-transfer resource fix.

AI-generated ordinary REST receivers use application methods, excluding CONNECT. The listener rejects unsupported method names explicitly. Older configurations containing unsupported methods show a warning and a **Remove unsupported methods** action in Studio, preserving the supported selections. Successful CONNECT requires tunnel semantics and is not implemented as an ordinary hosted API response. See [HTTP CONNECT semantics](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-9.3.6).
For test-only FTP coverage, install `pyftpdlib` in an isolated environment; it is not a shipped runtime dependency. Run from `backend`:

python -m unittest tests.test_input_xpath_and_connectors tests.test_transfer_network tests.test_amqp_jdbc_excel_command tests.test_product_hardening tests.test_snowflake tests.test_postgresql_examples
Additional qualification tests:
python -m unittest tests.test_connector_production tests.test_jdbc_callable tests.test_mysql_live

Set `MINA_TEST_MYSQLD` to an installed `mysqld` executable to enable the disposable MySQL tests. Without it, those tests explicitly skip. The test environment needs PyMySQL and cryptography; FTPS tests additionally need test-only pyftpdlib and pyOpenSSL. The JDBC harness requires `java` and `javac`. Rebuild the Java bridge with the standard Studio build scripts when distributing the updated JDBC code.

References: [Python FTP/FTPS](https://docs.python.org/3/library/ftplib.html), [Paramiko SFTP](https://docs.paramiko.org/en/stable/api/sftp.html), [Paramiko SSH](https://docs.paramiko.org/en/stable/api/client.html), and [Psycopg transactions](https://www.psycopg.org/psycopg3/docs/basic/transactions.html).
MINA documentation site and PDF

Open **Help > MINA Documentation** in Studio, or visit `/help/index.html` on the same host and port as Studio. No separate documentation service is required. Installed desktop Studio uses its existing local runtime address; do not assume a fixed port.

The documentation includes a searchable, expandable index and deep links to individual topics and tabs. Use **Download PDF** for the complete offline manual, or **Print topic** for the selected topic, including all its tabs. Light and dark display modes are supported.
Coverage and accuracy

Activity Configuration, Input, Output, Advanced and Errors sections are generated from Studio's base contracts and documentation definitions. Tasks, groups, mapping, functions, shared connections, deployment, debugging, administration and security guides are included. Project-selected schemas, provider modes and JDBC parameters can change the fields shown in Studio: the reference does not substitute for those project-specific schemas. Provider prerequisites and production qualification still apply.

Only explicitly selected product source files and guides are read. The generator does not inspect project data, environment credentials or user payloads. Existing implementation limitations are documented, not claimed as implemented.
Project Explorer and task canvas

New projects start with a Sub Task containing Start and End. Use a Starter Task when an external event, such as HTTP, a timer, or a message, starts the workflow. Use **Call Sub Task** to invoke reusable logic. Starter and Sub Task icons distinguish the two in Project Explorer.

Subtasks and **Call Sub Task** use the same process-network-and-bent-arrow symbol in Project Explorer, task tabs, creation menus, the activity picker, and the canvas. Starter tasks use the process network with a play symbol.

The canvas, activity palette, and activity picker share one activity icon catalog. Shared connections use the same protocol or vendor artwork in Project Explorer and connection creation menus. Imported legacy Mapper activities retain the Mapper symbol; an unrecognized activity uses a neutral process symbol instead of a Start or End icon.

Tasks, shared connections, and schemas belong to packages. Right-click their category or an existing package and choose **New Package** to create a top-level or nested folder. Choose the package when creating an item. **Default** is available for each category. Right-click an existing item and choose **Move to Package** to organize it without changing its references. Studio replaces spaces with hyphens in object names.

To rename a package, right-click the folder under **Tasks**, **Resources → Connections**, or **Schemas** and choose **Rename Package**. Its nested folders and items move with it, keeping task, connection, and schema references intact. Under **Packaging**, right-click the deployment artifact and choose **Rename Package** to update its name for future exports while keeping its version and settings. Save the project to keep these changes.

Task, connection, and schema names must be unique within the same package. Studio ignores case and treats spaces as hyphens when checking a name. You can reuse a name in a different package. For dynamic **Call Sub Task** routing, use the task ID or the qualified name (for example, `Orders/Validate`) if more than one subtask has the same name. **Validate Project** reports conflicts already present in older projects.
Package contents appear below their folder. If a name is shortened in a narrow Project Explorer, hover over it to see the full name or drag the pane divider to widen it.

When you first add a protocol activity or shared connection, Studio adds the relevant missing environment properties. Connection setup also offers those properties for binding. Review the generated defaults in the active environment before running the task.

Use **Magnify orchestrator** on the canvas and hover to see a 2× preview. Press Escape to turn it off. Select a transition to set its **Line color** or choose **Reset color** to restore the default. Close task tabs individually or use **Close All** to clear the canvas.

Use the **Theme** selector to change how Studio looks and feels. **Compact Workbench** uses a shorter ribbon and denser explorer rows. **Blueprint Board** uses a drafting grid and framed canvas activities. **Reading Room** uses larger labels, wider spacing, and a paper-like canvas. Existing themes are still available, and Studio remembers your choice.

The bottom-right **Runtime status** shows startup stages, current Studio operations, and the activities running in the active project. Click it for the designer and runtime details, including parallel activities and the latest detected slow UI operation on supported browsers. Startup progress counts completed stages; an animated bar means the operation has no reliable percentage. The Windows startup screen also shows the current stage before the designer is ready.

The footer and details use the same live runtime health check. If an older runtime does not provide activity-progress details, Studio reports that limitation separately. It does not mark a healthy runtime as unavailable.

The welcome screen shows packets moving along the integration routes. Use **Pause route animation** to stop them or **Play route animation** to start them. Until you choose a setting, the packets follow the Windows or browser reduced-motion preference. Studio remembers your choice.
JDBC query and writes

Use `:name` parameters for Query, Update, and Insert, and map each value under **Input → parameters**. To execute multiple records together, enable **Batch update** and map **records**. An empty list writes zero rows. For **Insert if record does not exist**, map an INSERT statement to **InsertStatement** and provide the parameters used by both statements. MINA runs the INSERT only when the UPDATE affects zero rows. If you need an atomic upsert across concurrent executions, use your database's native upsert statement.

To page through a query, enable **Process result in subsets** and use a stable `ORDER BY`. Start with **Row offset** zero. Pass the previous result's **nextRowOffset** to the next call and stop when **lastSubset** is true. **Maximum rows** caps the total rows across those pages. Each call re-executes the query.
PostgreSQL samples
Run [postgresql-setup.sql](/samples/postgresql-setup.sql) in a disposable PostgreSQL database. It creates `mina_demo.orders` and the `mina_demo.order_total` procedure.

In Studio **Samples**, open **PostgreSQL CRUD** or **PostgreSQL Procedure and Paging**. Set the JDBC URL, username, and password in the local environment. Use **Debug** to run the example Sub Task or run it by task ID in an exported Python archive.
CRUD upserts a demo row, updates it with a version guard, queries the JSONB field, and deletes that row. The other sample reads the first page and calls the procedure with an INOUT numeric argument.

PostgreSQL accepts libpq connection strings and JDBC-style PostgreSQL URLs. Configure **PostgreSQL TLS mode** and a trusted root certificate for verified TLS. A configured **Schema** becomes the search path. Use named `:parameter` bindings to avoid ambiguity with PostgreSQL's JSONB question-mark operator. Declare JSON or JSONB, ISO date/time, and decimal types for driver adaptation. To retain exact decimal digits from a mapped value, provide it as a string. Use JDBC Query with `SELECT` for PostgreSQL functions and Call Procedure for `CALL` operations. PostgreSQL statement timeout applies when configured on the activity.
Updating the guide
From the repository root, install the documentation authoring dependencies into your chosen Python environment:

python -m pip install -r scripts/documentation-requirements.txt
cd frontend
npm run docs:build
npm run docs:check
node --test scripts/documentation.test.mjs
If Python is not on PATH, set `MINA_DOCS_PYTHON` to its executable path before running `docs:build`. The Python dependencies are build-time only, not required to read the site or PDF.

`npm run build` checks that the generated documentation matches the selected source files. After changing those sources, regenerate the guide. The site and PDF are copied from `frontend/public/help` to `frontend/dist/help` by Vite and included in the normal Studio distribution. Rebuild the frontend and installer to deliver updated documentation to installed machines. Keep the whole help directory together when copying it for offline use; opening `index.html` directly also works without a server.

The guide is local to the Studio host. Making it reachable on a shared enterprise URL requires publishing these static assets through your approved web server and access controls; this change does not create a public internet endpoint.
MINA Integration Libraries
Open **Project Explorer → Libraries** to publish reusable subtasks, connections, and schemas, or to add a released version to an application.
Create and export a library

In the authoring project, build callable **Sub Tasks** and define their input and output contracts. Put environment-specific values in project properties and reference those properties from the assets.
Open **Libraries → Create a library**. Enter the display name, library ID, version, and an optional description.

Select the subtasks, connections, or schemas that other projects should see. MINA includes dependencies reached by fixed task and resource references as internal assets. It also includes selected Data Format assets and schemas reached through local XSD includes or relative JSON Schema references.
Select **Publish version**, then **Export .mlib**. Use a new three-part version number for revised content. Repeating publication of the same content is safe.

The archive contains the published asset definitions, declared setting types, and a checksum. Project environment values are omitted. Use property references for credentials and URLs that contain credentials. Bindings used by recognized connector credential fields are created as password properties. Move project-only custom function calls out of a subtask before publishing. Library publication reports them because those functions need a definition in the consuming project.
Use one release in multiple projects
Open **Libraries → Use a library**. Choose a release from the catalog or use **Import .mlib file**.
Enter a project alias and select **Add to project**. The alias qualifies the names in the task, connection, and schema selectors.
Set the generated `library.<alias>.<setting>` values under **Properties** in each environment you run or package. Each project owns its environment values, secret bindings, and connection instances.
Use **Call Sub Task** to map input to an exported task, choose an exported connection from the connector dropdown, or choose an exported schema in a compatible schema picker.

Map the task's public input and output schemas in **Call Sub Task**. Installed library tasks appear by name and version. Debug measures the call as one activity and shows the caller's input, result, and any failure at that boundary. Explicit messages published by the library's Log activities can appear in the application log.

Each project pins the exact version and checksum. To change a version, choose the new release with the same alias, select **Review version change**, and apply the change after reviewing the exported contracts and binding changes. Compatible upgrades preserve existing references. To roll back, select the previous version using the same process. References to a removed or private export must be remapped before the change can be applied.
Use **Export .mlib** beside an installed release to export the exact pinned version, including after reopening a workspace on a different Studio installation.
Samples included in the catalog

rows: Pass a message and correlation ID to WriteLog. From a Catch branch, pass the code, message, and correlation ID to HandleException. Map its structured result and decide in the calling flow whether to route, retry, or rethrow.
Bind `library.enterprise-connections.database-path` to a SQLite database path and select Database in a JDBC Query. Local-EMS uses an in-process queue for local examples.

blocks.text: To try reuse, add both releases to two projects. Point each project's `database-path` binding at a different SQLite file and call Operations from both flows. The library versions stay the same while the JDBC results follow each project's binding.
Share through Control Plane or deployment packages

Open **Control Plane catalog** under **Use a library**. Enter the Control Plane URL, credential, and team ID as applicable. Select a local release and choose **Publish selected release** to share it with the team. Use **Load catalog** and **Download to Studio** to import an authorized team's release. Add that release to the project to create its version pin.

Studio workspace exports carry library IDs, versions, aliases, and checksums. On a different Studio backend, install those exact `.mlib` releases before opening the workspace. Older workspace exports with embedded releases still open. Run and Debug resolve the implementation on the backend. Application packaging includes the implementation for execution on the data plane.
Protect files shared with application developers

For a managed Studio, set `MINA_LIBRARY_ARCHIVE_KEY` on the publishing and consuming Studio backends to the same operator-managed, Base64-encoded 32-byte key. Studio exports authenticated encrypted `.mlib` files in this mode. The Control Plane library catalog transports them without the key. Keep the key in the backend's secret configuration and share the archive with developers. Studio can still import legacy `.mlib` files. Republish an existing Control Plane version to replace its legacy archive with the encrypted form. Treat earlier plaintext copies as source-bearing.

In managed mode, deploy projects that use libraries through the approved HTTPS Control Plane. Set `MINA_LIBRARY_CONTROL_PLANE_URL` on Studio to that base URL. Studio requires TLS verification and disables downloading the deployment archive directly for those projects. Limit access to deployment packages and runtime hosts to operators who can see their contents. Backend administrators and workloads with unrestricted access to the backend filesystem can read the installed implementation. On workstations without a managed key, library files and deployment packages are portable source-bearing archives.

When a **Call Sub Task** target comes from a project property, fill in that property for each packaged environment or set a fixed fallback. Packaging includes the referenced subtasks for every selected profile.

pages.title: XML JSON and Data parse and render activities

blocks.text: XML JSON and Data parse and render activities

All six Parse/Render XML, JSON and Data activities use one implementation in Studio, Direct Python archives and Engine Python archives. **Configuration** contains design selectors and checkboxes. Map documents, paths, encodings, delimiters, fixed offsets, root names, JSON formatting and other runtime values in **Input → formatOptions**. A mapped option takes precedence over the checkbox, activity default or shared Data Format value. Existing text settings appear as editable Input mappings; Studio migrates them when you edit the mappings. Attach project or inline schemas in the Input/Output Editor.
XML

Parse XML accepts text, base64 binary or dynamic input. Map binary input to `xmlBinary.bytes` and optionally supply `xmlBinary.forceEncoding` and `xmlBinary.byteCount`. Without an override, Parse XML uses the byte order mark or XML declaration. Attributes use `@name`, schema-defined repeating elements are arrays even with one occurrence, and ordered mixed text and child elements use `#content`.

Render XML accepts a parsed wrapper or a mapped schema tree. In Configuration, choose text or binary and set the default validation, declaration, indentation and namespace options. In Input, map `byteEncoding` for binary output and `formatOptions.cdataElements` for CDATA. The CDATA picker can insert paths from the selected input schema. Binary output includes `xmlBytes`, plus the existing MINA `binaryContent`, `bytes`, `byteCount` and `encoding` fields.

Validate parsed output and Validate input tree perform XSD validation, including required children, attributes and datatypes. Select the entry XSD as the activity schema. Keep its `xs:include` and `xs:import` dependencies as project schema assets with the relative filenames used by `schemaLocation`. An import without a location resolves only when there is one project XSD for that namespace. The schema tree and both Python archives use the same project assets.

The resolver is offline: URLs, local machine paths, traversal outside the project, DTDs, entities, XSD redefine and override are rejected. XML input is limited to 64 MiB; each XSD to 8 MiB and a dependency graph to 32 MiB. Namespace URIs and mixed text are preserved structurally; serialized prefixes, whitespace and lexical formatting need not match the original bytes.

Binary XML output preserves characters outside the selected encoding using numeric XML character references. For CDATA-selected text, references are emitted outside the CDATA sections so parsing restores the original value. Literal ampersands and `]]>` content retain their values. A CDATA selector can be a schema path such as `record.notes` or an expanded element name such as `{urn:example}notes`. Expanded names match both the namespace and local name. Imported binary render bindings can carry a mapped byte encoding alongside the XML document. MINA uses that encoding and serializes the document inside the binding. Schema-tree mappings with expanded namespace names are ordered according to the XSD and retain qualified attributes. Unknown input or output styles raise a validation error.
JSON
Select the conversion mode under **Configuration → Schema type**:

**Native JSON** is the existing MINA mode. It parses and renders objects, arrays and primitive values directly. It supports offline JSON Schema validation with local references, and can omit null object fields without changing array positions.

**Generic** converts between a JSON string and an XML string without a schema. With Badgerfish selected, namespaces use `@xmlns`, attributes use `@name` and text uses `$`. Generic Render JSON treats XML text as strings unless **Infer numeric and boolean values** is enabled.

**XSD** converts between JSON and a schema-defined XML tree. Select an XSD in Parse JSON's Output Editor or Render JSON's Input Editor. Validation is on by default. **Ignore additional JSON fields** filters unknown input fields when validation is enabled. An array declared by the XSD remains an array even when only one value is present.

New JSON activities default to **XSD**. Existing activities without a saved mode continue to use **Native JSON**. The JSON root styles are **None**, **JSON with Root** and **Anonymous Array**. For Anonymous Array in XSD mode, the root must have one repeating child. **Use null for empty values** represents empty containers as nil when there is an XML container. Parse JSON rejects malformed JSON and non-finite numbers; its duplicate-key policy supports First wins, Last wins and Error. Render JSON can format the result and exposes the serialized output as `jsonString`.

XSD simple-content types retain their primitive text datatype, including inheritance from another simple-content type. A type with attributes exposes its text as `#text` in XML schema-tree mappings, alongside `@attribute` fields. Parse JSON's normalized output aliases expose the same text as `$` and attributes without `@`; Studio source paths match those aliases. A simple-content value with no attributes is a primitive field. XML boolean text accepts the whitespace permitted by its XSD datatype.

On Render JSON, explicitly mapped schema-tree fields take precedence over a predecessor's serialized XML wrapper. Mapping only `formatOptions` changes formatting or conversion settings without replacing the payload. **Use empty values for null** substitutes empty containers for schema-typed nil objects/arrays; nil primitives remain JSON `null`, including primitive items in repeating fields, preserving array positions. Empty simple-content strings with attributes remain explicit text values.
Delimited and fixed-width Data

Parse Data accepts a string or runtime file path with a selected encoding. Map `text` or `fileName` in Input. Use `skipHeaderCharacters` to bypass a preamble, `noOfRecords` to limit a batch (`-1` means all records), and `startRecord` for a zero-based manual offset. If you leave the offset unmapped, each batch advances the same activity's cursor within that task execution. Use `done` to exit a loop and `nextRecord` when supplying your own offset. **Continue on record errors** returns invalid field values or column counts in `ErrorRows.error`; an invalid document structure, such as an unterminated quoted field, still fails.
Configure the format inline or add a JSON schema asset under **Project Explorer → Schemas** with a `dataFormat` object. Select it as **Shared Data Format** on both activities. For example:
{"dataFormat":{"format":"delimited","delimiter":",","header":true,"fields":"id,name","fieldTypes":"integer,string","strictColumns":true}}

An optional `schemaId` links the shared format to a project row schema. Parse Data exposes typed `records`, `Rows.schema`, record counts and the XML representation. Render Data accepts mapped records and exposes the rendered value as `text`, `Text` and `content`.

To reuse an existing layout, right-click **Schemas** and choose **Import XSD or Data Format**. Select a Data Format XML resource (`.dataformat`, `.dataformatresource` or `.dataformatsharedresource`) or a ZIP containing it and its companion XSDs. ZIP entries retain their relative paths. The importer converts delimited and fixed layouts into reusable MINA assets and links supported Parse/Render Data references in imported processes.

A source module property bound to the Data Format column separator becomes a MINA environment property and an editable **Input → formatOptions → Column separator** mapping. Import the ZIP with its `default.substvar` and, if available, `local.substvar`, `dev.substvar`, `qa.substvar`, `pre.substvar` or `production.substvar`. A profile value overrides the default, which falls back to the resource's literal separator if present. If no value is available, set the imported property before running. Select the imported Data Format on both activities to add its mapping without overwriting custom mappings. Unsupported substitution targets and ambiguous or secret profile values are reported during import.

Quoted CSV values retain delimiters, escaped quotes and embedded line breaks. Literal multi-character delimiters and any-character separator sets also support quoting. Render Data exposes both `content` and `text` for mapping into HTTP bodies, files or subsequent activities. Headers, line endings and final separators are configurable.

Fixed-width records use positive widths or zero-based `start:end` offsets (end excluded), so columns can have gaps. The optional fixed line length includes the separator. Numeric fields use left padding and preserve significant trailing zeroes. Strict mode rejects over-width values; permissive mode retains truncation. Single-character delimited and fixed-width files are read record by record; the multi-character delimiter reader has a 64 MiB limit. Use Mapper for hierarchy and complex transformations.
Data validation and layout safeguards

Parse Data and Render Data now have an optional **Validate records against selected XSD** checkbox. The equivalent dynamic Input options are `formatOptions.validateOutput` for parsing and `formatOptions.validateInput` for rendering. Validation uses the complete record XML and selected project or inline XSD, including packaged imports/includes, required fields, numeric facets, string constraints and namespaces. Validation is off by default for existing Data activities. Enabling it without an XSD fails explicitly. JSON Schema field inference does not substitute for XSD record validation.

Validation runs on the parsed batch or on the structured render input before formatting. It does not validate the truncated text of a permissive fixed-width render; enable strict mode to prevent truncation. If all records are rejected or the batch is empty, an XSD requiring at least one row can reject the batch.

Declared field names and types are matched by name when a CSV header is in a different order. Under **Require exact record fields**, headers must contain the declared names, with no missing/extra fields; a different order is allowed. Without strict mode, legacy unmatched headers retain positional type fallback. Empty or duplicate field/header names are rejected. Header names remain case sensitive. This prevents an integer type intended for `id` being applied to the `name` column merely because the source changed column order.

Strict rendering requires every declared field and rejects extra fields for single-character, multi-character and fixed layouts. An explicit null field remains distinct from a missing mapping and renders empty/padded text under existing rules. Fixed numeric zero-fill keeps a negative sign at the front (`-12` at width five becomes `-0012`).

Automatic batch cursors now reset when field types, fixed offsets/length, trimming, fill, strictness, validation/schema or record-error handling changes, as well as when the source/header/separator changes. Changing batch size alone continues from the current position. Task runs retain separate cursor state.

Unknown format, separator rule, blank-line policy and line-separator options fail rather than silently falling back to a different interpretation. Supported line-separator selectors are Auto, LF, CRLF and CR.

**Nested record structures** preserves parent paths and repeating JSON-valued columns. **Stream large files** parses to JSON Lines or renders JSON Lines to a formatted file in byte/count-bounded batches, returning file/count metadata. Multi-character separators use the same bounded reader. **Continue on record errors** now supports bounded malformed-quote recovery and physical-line mode, with explicit rejected-record reporting. Recovery cannot remove the inherent ambiguity of missing quotes; select the policy matching the source contract. See [nested records and streaming](DATA_NESTED_STREAMING.md) for Input mappings, validation scope, limits, atomic output behavior and complete-flow measurements. Streaming activities also support explicit **Group header/detail/trailer records**, **Validate whole-file rules** and **Validate complete file against XSD**. Map role layouts, trailer controls, file counts/totals, unique keys and root attributes dynamically in Input. Global XSD validation runs through EOF before publication, replacing batch-only checks for that stream. See the [HDT and whole-file guide](DATA_GROUPS_VALIDATION.md).
See [gap verification](validation/mapper-data-gaps-summary-2026-11-16.json) and [changed files](MAPPER_DATA_GAPS_CHANGED_FILES.md).
Dynamic HTTP and REST invocation settings
HTTP Request and REST Invoke Configuration keeps the display name and shared connection selector. Request-specific settings are mapped in **Input → RestInputRequest**:

RestInputRequest
  Config
    host, port, scheme, requestURI, Method, RequestBody, bodyFormat
    QueryParameters, URIParameters, QueryString, FilePath
    timeout, activityTimeoutSeconds, followRedirects, raiseForStatus
    openApiDocument, operationId, openApiBaseUrl
    openApiReferenceDocuments, openApiAllowedRefOrigins
    validateRequest, requestSchema, validateResponse, responseSchema
  Headers
    accept, content-type, Accept-Charset, Accept-Encoding, Cookie, pragma
  CustomHeaders[] → name, value
  mimeEnvelopeElement
    mimePart[] → mimeHeaders, binaryContent | textContent | fileName

Map constants, properties, upstream values or functions. String literals require quotes; booleans use `true`/`false`. Contract/schema fields accept JSON objects or quoted JSON/YAML/XSD text as appropriate. Operation IDs select the contract operation, whose method/path are authoritative. Empty custom schema overrides use the contract.

Previously saved Configuration values appear as typed Input mappings without a manual migration. Listener routing, server connections and security policies remain startup settings because they must exist before a request arrives. Keep external-reference origins restricted to trusted values; empty disables network reference retrieval.
Verification

The tests cover binary encoding overrides, CDATA, XML namespaces, XSD import/include resolution and access boundaries, Generic and XSD JSON conversion, Data Format import, dynamic Input mappings, rejected records, batching, multiline CSV and fixed offsets. All six activities run in fresh Direct and Engine archives and are compared with Studio Run and Debug.
Imported processes

Import a compatible process ZIP from Studio. MINA can retain XML and JSON Parse/Render steps and their original XSLT input bindings. Selected XSD elements are resolved by namespace and local name, including schemas embedded in the process. When a connector blocks full process conversion, the import can recover supported Mapper and format activities as separate subtasks. Supply each recovered activity's original input variables by name. Studio reports unbound Parse Data resources and empty input bindings.
From `backend`, with its Python environment:
python -m unittest tests.test_format_activities tests.test_http_dynamic_contracts tests.test_ai_exception_data tests.test_raw_python tests.test_engine_export tests.test_activity_packs -q
References: [Python CSV newline handling](https://docs.python.org/3/library/csv.html) and [lxml parsing and validation](https://lxml.de/apidoc/lxml.etree.html).
Selecting the XSD entry structure

When an XSD contains several global elements or named complex types, choose the required **Structure** beside the schema selector. This choice controls the activity's Input/Output tree, XML root, schema-derived record fields and runtime validation. Other declarations stay available as dependencies and as choices; they are not shown as additional mapping roots. The selected entry is retained in Run, Debug and both Python export formats. Imported schema text is hidden; inline source editing is available explicitly through **Edit inline schema**.
Transformation and mediation capabilities
The Mapper remains the transformation activity. General activities provide durable message composition and recovery without reintroducing Mediation.
Mapper schemas and suggestions
Select one XSD structure

After choosing a project XSD, use **Target structure** to select one global element or named complex type. The Input and Output trees show only that entry and its descendants. A named complex type receives a document wrapper named after the type; choose an existing global element when its published XML root name is required. Source schemas and named source views have the same selection.

This selection is also available for task input/return interfaces (including Call Sub Task), Parse/Render XML, JSON and Data contracts, and HTTP/REST request and response schemas. Each activity retains its own choice when saved, reopened, run, debugged or exported as either Python archive format.

Selected project schemas display their filename and structure controls instead of a populated XSD textbox. **Edit inline schema** explicitly opens inline content editing. Opening an existing schema resource starts on **Schema Structure**; **XSD Source** remains available for deliberate source editing.

MINA retains the original declarations for changing selections and resolving references. Its selection metadata is a namespaced XSD annotation attribute; validation compiles the selected declaration and its dependencies. Unselected entry roots are excluded from the mapping tree and generated API schema. Missing types used by the selected structure remain validation errors.

The Mapper supports multiple named views of one source, each with its own schema, optional XSD complex type, and occurrence range. Keep schema files at their project-relative paths when importing or editing the contract. The Mapper resolves imports and includes from project assets. A repeating element stays an array in the structured result even when the generated XML has one occurrence; the XML itself retains the original element structure.

In **Visual AI Mapper → AI mapping options**, choose **Exact names** or a similarity strategy. Select a source or target branch to limit matching to that branch, then set each side's search depth from 1 to 10 (default 4). Leave a side on **Entire schema** to search all fields on that side. Existing manual mappings are preserved.
Drop a repeating structure
On Mapper **Input**, drag a repeating complex source onto a repeating complex target and choose **Finish** after selecting a mapping mode:

**Make a copy of each** copies the whole collection. The target shows one **[Copy-Of]** row with its source expression and hides the children. Existing child mappings in that occurrence are replaced. Clear the copy to show the children again. Use this when the source items already match the target structure.

**For each** adds a **[For-Each]** row for the collection and keeps the item and its children visible. Matching paths are filled in without regard to case. Children display expressions relative to the current item, such as `Name` or `Address.City`, and remain editable.
**SmartMap** builds an editable loop and also matches child paths that differ by underscores or hyphens. Ambiguous matches are left unmapped.

The same three choices are available on other activity **Input** tabs and in **Edit mappings** when both structures expose repeating records. This includes **Call Sub Task** inputs and **End** return mappings when the task has a schema. Drops onto simple fields still map the value directly.

To add another source for a repeating target, right-click the row and choose **Duplicate mapping**. This works in Mapper and other activity Input editors, including **Call Sub Task** and **End**. You can duplicate an unmapped repeating field too. The new occurrence starts with empty bindings. Drop a different collection onto it and choose a mapping mode for complex records. The original keeps its source and child bindings. At runtime the original items come first, followed by the configured duplicates in order. An occurrence with no source adds no items.

Right-click a complex element and choose **Delete mapping** to clear its binding and all mappings below it, even when only its children are mapped. Nested repeating occurrences within that branch are cleared too. The schema structure stays available for remapping. This works in Mapper and other activity Input editors, including HTTP responses, Call Sub Task and End. Deleting a duplicate occurrence keeps the original and sibling occurrences unchanged.
Use **Map & Test** to check the generated result before running or exporting the flow.
XML expressions and bindings

In any activity's **Input → Functions → XPath functions**, choose XPath 1.0 or 2.0, expand a category, select a function and fill its XPath arguments. Quote text arguments, for example `'text'`; XML paths and numeric expressions need no text quotes. Drag the prepared expression onto a target. Type a function prefix in a field for XPath suggestions. Mapper has additional XML source/namespace settings; other inputs can pass an explicit XML source with `xpath2("expression", ${input.xmlString})`.

The designer includes the complete supported catalog even when the runtime palette request is unavailable: 49 XPath 1.0 signatures and 201 XPath 2.0 signatures, including overloads. Categories include strings, regular expressions, numbers, sequences, booleans, date/time, nodes/namespaces, URI encoding and XML Schema constructors. The general Mapper functions remain available in the same Functions tab.

The **XPath expression builder** offers the same categorized inventory, search, argument labels and descriptions. **Expression XPath version** selects the version for that field; applying it saves an explicit `xpath1(...)` or `xpath2(...)` expression. Existing fields keep their saved XPath versions. Use operators such as `+`, `-`, `*`, `div`, `mod`, `=`, `!=`, `<` and `>` directly in the expression. Functions that retrieve external documents or collections are not exposed by this offline runtime.

In Mapper **Configuration**, choose the XPath version and expand **XML expressions and runtime binding**. Set the XML source to a mapping path such as `${last.xmlString}`, or leave it empty to use the previous activity's XML output. Add namespace prefixes and variables as JSON objects. For example, `{"ord":"urn:orders"}` binds a namespace and `{"minimum":"${input.minimum}"}` binds a value to `$minimum`.

In **Input**, enter an expression such as `xpath('string(/ord:orders/ord:order[@id=$minimum]/@id)')`. The **XPath expression builder** can test a raw formula against sample XML or a JSON envelope and apply it to the selected target. Choose a function to display its arguments. Drag a sample XML field into an argument, or select the field and use the argument's button. In XPath 2.0, the target cast action wraps the current formula in the target's supported XML Schema constructor. XPath node selections return sequences. Use an XPath scalar function when the target expects one value. Map & Test accepts raw XML or a JSON input envelope. XPath resource loading is disabled. XPath 2.0 regex functions run in an isolated worker with a deadline.

Import an `.xsl` or `.xslt` file or edit the binding directly to select manual XSLT. A manual XSLT 1.0 or 2.0 binding publishes `xmlString` and structured XML values. Select a target XSD to validate the generated XML. Referenced XSDs must be present in project schemas under their declared locations. Stylesheets run with file and network access disabled. XML inputs, stylesheets, and parsed results are limited to 8 MiB per document. XSLT 2.0 runs in a separate SaxonC worker with a scrubbed environment and a deadline. The configured XML variables also supply stylesheet parameters. XSLT 2.0 accepts XML-valued parameters as document nodes.

In **Configuration**, use **Source type overrides** to coerce specific source paths before formulas and XML parameter binding. For example, `{"input.order.amount":"decimal"}` converts the input amount to a number.

In **Input → Source coercions and cardinality**, create named views of the same source path. Set optional, exactly one, repeating, or at least one. Select a project schema to copy its contract into the view, or enter an inline contract. For XML, a named complex type must be valid for the source element's declaration. For JSON, the selected contract validates each occurrence. Choose a view or one of its fields from Data Sources. Occurrence ranges and type validation apply when a rule reads that view. Source views run in visual mapping mode.

In the XPath builder, use **Check XPath 1.0 quick fix** or **Check XPath 2.0 quick fix** to compare the two evaluations. Apply a passing fix to the selected visual mapping. Other mappings keep their existing XPath version. A matching sample result does not establish equivalence for every possible input.

In **Input → Open visual AI Mapper**, use **Download XSLT** to save the active stylesheet or generate XSLT 2.0 from direct rules. Generation supports XML element paths, scalar constants, If, Choose, For-Each, For-Each-Group, nested loops, and duplicate loop occurrences with mapped children. It supports trim, normalize space, and case conversion. A selected XSD must have one root and a uniform element qualification policy. Supply an XML sample with the named document root for testing. Use **Open XSLT** to restore the editable mappings from a generated file. **Use generated XSLT** binds execution to the current visual rules. **Generated XML binding preferences** controls optional field existence checks, suppression when a nil source maps to an optional non-nillable target, and copying `xsi:nil` to nillable targets. Generated conditions accept XML field paths, scalar literals, comparisons, and logical operators. Custom functions and mapping statements outside this subset require a handwritten stylesheet.

The XPath builder provides extension functions such as `ext:trim`, `upper-case`, `lower-case`, `left`, `right`, `concat-sequence`, `xor`, `substring-before-last`, `substring-after-last`, `timestamp`, `base64-to-hex`, and `hex-to-base64`. `project:getModuleProperty` reads scalar MINA project properties supplied to the execution. Java system properties, proprietary extensions, and custom Java XPath functions require a separate migration.
Legacy process import

Open a compatible process file or ZIP through Studio's project import. Supported sequences, simple scopes, conditional XPath links, no-match links, error links, static subtask calls, Mapper bindings, XML render, file activities, and basic outbound HTTP requests become MINA activities. Supported HTTP, JMS and Timer event definitions become native starters. HTTP XML reply bindings become response activities. The importer also reads supported HTTP client and server settings, non-XA JDBC resources and static SQL activities, and JMS text-message activities with direct or JNDI connections. Passwords are represented by empty deployment properties. Project XSDs are included. Check the import messages in Studio for processes and settings that need review. Unsupported processes can contribute standalone Mapper tasks for their recoverable bindings. Supply original activity variables as task input for these standalone tasks. REST/SOAP service descriptors, explicit BPEL join expressions, XA transactions, vendor-specific JDBC/JMS features, and proprietary transport policies still need manual conversion.
Shared Smart Mapper learning

Use **Share reviewed mappings** in Visual AI Mapper after reviewing direct field mappings. The Studio server stores field paths and schema fingerprints. Recommendations for the same source and target schema rank shared field pairs first. Disabled rules, pending suggestions, formulas, and literal values are excluded from learning. The catalog is stored in the Studio server's data directory and is available to Studio users connected to that server.
Both Python archive formats include `requirements-mapper.txt` when they use XML bindings. Install those dependencies in the target runtime before running the archive.
Mapper tests, templates and contracts

Open **Map & Test** and expand **Saved transformation tests**. Give each case a name, an input JSON value and an independently reviewed expected JSON value. Save the case and run the suite. Failures show field paths, expected/actual values and contract errors in dark red. Tests remain in the activity config and survive project save/export/import. They do not call connectors.

**Versioned templates and schema changes** exports a `.mtemplate.json` file containing schemas, mapping rules, lookup tables, execution policies, custom functions and test cases. Templates have a format version and content checksum; the checksum detects corruption, not authenticity. Import a template into another Mapper. Project schema IDs are cleared because IDs are project-specific. Local history retains the last 20 exported versions; changed content requires a new version. Restore a version, review its contract and rerun its tests.

Capture a contract baseline before changing the selected schema. Compare the current contract to see added/removed/changed fields, affected target mappings and raw contract changes. This reports changes; it is not a full backward compatibility proof for every schema dialect.

The portable validator now checks JSON `pattern`, `patternProperties`, common formats, conditional contracts (`if`/`then`/`else`), dependent required fields, property names and `contains` counts, in addition to the previous checks. Supported asserted formats are date, date-time, time, IPv4, IPv6, UUID, email, hostname and URI; unknown formats remain annotations. Pattern matching has a 100 ms timeout and requires the `regex` package, declared in deployment qualification when a schema uses patterns. XSD restrictions support enumeration, length bounds, numeric bounds and digit constraints. XSD patterns use the portable regex dialect with full matching; XML Schema-specific regex syntax and complete JSON Schema/XSD conformance are not claimed.
Lookups, enrichment and joins
Save named JSON lookup tables under **Lookup tables and execution limits**:
{"countries": {"US": "United States", "IN": "India"}}

Use `lookupTable(${input.country}, "countries", "Unknown")` in Mapper, or append a `lookupTable("countries", "Unknown")` pipeline step. Keys are case-sensitive. `lookup(value, table, default)` accepts an object table directly; `enrich(record, fields)` merges objects with enrichment fields taking precedence; `joinBy(left, right, leftKey, rightKey)` produces matching merged records; `chunks(records, size)` splits an array into batches. Missing join keys do not match. Many-to-many joins stop at 100,000 result records.
Large data and cancellation

Mapper has evaluation-step, execution-time and output-size limits. Defaults are 100,000 evaluation steps and 30 seconds. Execution runs in a worker thread; workflow cancellation signals the evaluator at subsequent evaluation checks. These are cooperative limits, not preemption of every individual function or vendor call. Input has target-field search and collapse/expand controls, so users can focus on a small portion of a large schema without losing mappings.
Both Python archive formats include:

python run_tests.py
Get-Content records.jsonl | python transform_jsonl.py --activity main/map --batch-size 100

`run_tests.py` runs saved suites and exits nonzero when any case fails or no saved suites exist. `transform_jsonl.py` processes one JSON record per line and prints one mapped JSON record per line. It runs Mapper alone, without connectors. Records are limited to 1 MB; batches default to 16 MB of serialized input/output and mapped records default to a 1 MB output limit. Use a smaller batch if the batch quota is exceeded. Output written before an error remains written; stage the output before publishing if all-or-nothing delivery is needed.
Durable message activities

Use an explicit **Message namespace** for each integration and the same **Durable state file** for cooperating activities. `MINA_MESSAGE_STATE_FILE` can provide the file globally; the default is `message-state.sqlite3` under `MINA_DATA_DIR` or the user's `.mina` folder. SQLite transactions coordinate processes sharing the same local file. For containers, mount durable storage. This is not a distributed database for multiple hosts or network filesystems. Payloads are capped at 1 MB, aggregate groups at 64 MB and state capacity defaults to 256 MB. Size accounting is an approximate SQLite page budget.
**Deduplicate Message** claims a stable message key and returns `accepted`
and `claimToken`. Route on `accepted`: process accepted messages, skip or acknowledge duplicate deliveries according to the connector policy.
**Message Receipt** completes the exact claim token after downstream success
or marks it failed on an error path. Stale/expired tokens cannot complete a newer claim. Acknowledge the broker only after successful work and receipt.
**Replay Messages** lists failed/expired candidates. `requeue` makes one

explicit key claimable again; it does not execute downstream activities. Feed the returned stored payload back through the normal task deliberately. `purge` removes expired completed keys and old completed aggregates; it keeps failed and pending messages. Completed keys default to seven-day retention.
**Aggregate Messages** appends messages with a stable message ID and

correlation key. Duplicate IDs do not increase the group count. When the expected count is reached, `ready=true` returns the records once; subsequent deliveries do not emit again. Check `ready` before forwarding. After a timeout, `flush` explicitly emits a partial group. A completed group needs a new correlation/window key for the next aggregation.
**Split Records** creates record batches from an array for use with the
existing For Each group. It is an in-memory activity; use the JSONL tool for streaming file transformations.

These primitives support reliable processing but cannot guarantee exactly-once external side effects. A crash between an external write and its receipt may require replay; make the downstream write idempotent using the stable key. Live broker/provider qualification remains necessary for production deployment.
Visual mapper and generated previews

Open Visual AI Mapper from Mapper Configuration. The left pane contains editable source test data and available source paths, the middle pane contains saved mappings and the complete selected target schema field list, and the right pane displays generated output after Run mapping test. Named XSD types and local JSON Schema references use the same field parser as the Input tab. Source expressions remain editable, including upstream activity references and functions. Schema text is available under the collapsed schema sections.

Map & Test also displays generated output directly after running. JSON targets show formatted JSON; XSD targets show an XML preview with repeating elements and the target namespace. The preview does not change the Mapper runtime object or exported archive behavior; use Render XML or render-xml when the downstream activity requires a serialized XML value. Test data and the latest output are retained when saving the visual mapper.
Activity debugging and testing
Job Data tree

The ribbon's **Job Data** window shows processes, call activities, and nested subtask activities in an expandable tree (initially expanded). Select a process or activity to inspect its captured input and output. Data is keyed by process and activity, not by a flattened activity ID. Completed calls record the actual called task, including dynamically resolved calls. Unexecuted activities are labelled as not captured. Repeated invocations show the latest captured values for that task/activity; this is not a per-invocation execution-history viewer.
Windows installations must be rebuilt and updated with the new installer to receive these UI/backend changes; restarting an older installation is insufficient.

During an active debug session, a dedicated Debug ribbon appears underneath the Studio ribbon. Its execution controls include Continue, Ignore Breakpoints, Pause, Stop, Step In/Over/Out, Run to Selected, Go to Current Activity, and Break on Next Event for a live listener. Its inspection tools include Thread Paths, Debug Metrics, Breakpoints, Watches, Variables, Evaluate, Job Data, Edit Payload, Preview Inputs, Test Activity, and Mock Output. Data/tool buttons open the relevant editor section; real tests and mocks still require explicit submission there. Commands are enabled according to session state. The ribbon disappears when the session completes, fails, or stops; it is not shown during ordinary Run mode.

Choose **Run → Start Activity Testing** to create a paused debug session and open the test bench. Unlike ordinary Debug, this does not automatically run the flow or start event listeners. The existing Debug Tools window also contains the bench.

Use the searchable process/activity tree on the left of the test bench. Expand a process or subprocess and select its activity; enter the input in the right pane. Each target retains its own input draft while the dialog remains open. Selecting a Call Sub Task row selects the call activity itself; expanding its arrow reveals the called subprocess and its activities. Nested calls can be expanded the same way, and selecting a nested activity targets its owning subprocess. Search includes nested activities. Circular references stop with a notice. Dynamic calls show a configured fallback, if any, labelled as potentially different from the runtime target; unresolved targets are not guessed.

Selecting a process targets its unique entry activity (or Start); Run once still executes only that entry activity, not the entire process. If the entry is ambiguous, select an activity explicitly. Independent tests can target another process in the debug project without moving the paused flow. Mock stepping is restricted to the current paused process and activity.

Select an activity and enter a JSON payload (including arrays, strings, numbers, or null), or choose raw text/XML. The test payload is available as both `input` and `last` for this independent test. Earlier activity outputs and environment properties remain available for mappings.
**Preview inputs** resolves configuration and mappings without executing the activity.
**Run once (real)** executes the selected activity without advancing the paused
flow. Inspect resolved inputs, output, logs, duration, and failure details.
**Use mock output & step** supplies the payload as the current paused activity's
output, skips its actual connector execution, and follows its normal transitions. Use this to simulate a receiver or downstream dependency without contacting it.
Optional **field overrides** are a JSON object keyed by the activity's configuration
field names, such as `message` or `topic`. They are applied after mappings as literal values. Preview first to verify the inputs.
Optional **assertions** use runtime conditions, for example `${last.count} > 0`.
Results distinguish execution failures from assertion failures.
