Python archive modes
Studio exposes two distinct Python exports. Both contain Python application files and `manifest.json` for Control Plane package metadata; neither includes project, task, or resource JSON descriptors.

**Export direct Python / Deploy direct Python** compiles supported task transitions into async Python state machines. The generated task source contains direct `if`/`elif` flow decisions, inline group conditions/loops, `asyncio.gather` for success fan-out, and typed Python references for property and activity bindings. It does not bundle the MINA workflow engine. The exporter rejects unsupported semantics with activity names instead of silently substituting an engine-backed implementation. Supported paths include Start, End, Scheduler, Log, Mapper (including functions, conditions, and repeating targets), Call Sub Task, global and transition Catch, Throw, Rethrow, General activities (Empty, Assign, Sleep, Checkpoint, shared variables, and External Command), File, FTP/SFTP, hosted and outbound HTTP/REST/SOAP, HTTP Response, XML/JSON/flat-data parse and render, Excel Read, Transform, Python/Java Invoke, JDBC, Snowflake, AMQP, Kafka, Pub/Sub, EMS/JMS send, receive, request/reply and reply, and supported SAP operations and IDoc parsing. Scheduler, Kafka, Pub/Sub, EMS, JMS, SAP, HTTP, REST, and SOAP starters remain active until stopped. SAP IDoc listeners support direct JCo and EMS/JMS/Kafka messaging sources. Single-entry/single-exit If, For Each, Iterate, While, Repeat, Repeat-on-Error, JDBC transaction, and critical-section groups compile to explicit Python control flow and may be nested with mixed group types. Client-acknowledge JMS receivers use a persistent bridge session and Confirm Message can acknowledge an active delivery.

**Python compatibility archive (engine-backed)** retains the full Python runtime engine and the existing wider activity/group behavior. It remains deployable but is not a full direct-code conversion. The package manifest records `pythonSource.mode: engine` so consumers can tell which implementation they received.

The standard `.mpkg` and `.ear` exports remain available. Python archives require separately licensed vendor drivers where the underlying connection needs them (for example SAP JCo or JMS/EMS). A Python source package does not replace those vendor libraries. Legacy `.ifpkg` packages remain importable.
File and AMQP starters

Both Python archive modes keep File Poller and AMQP Receive Message starter tasks active until stopped. A File Poller takes an initial snapshot of matching paths. Enable **Include existing files** to send those matches into the flow on the first scan. Later scans emit the configured Created, Modified, Deleted, or All events. An unchanged scan does not start a workflow. Each restart takes a fresh snapshot, so enabling **Include existing files** can reprocess files left in the directory. To map the name of the first matching file from a preceding poll, use `${last.files.0.fileName}`. Numeric segments in these paths use zero-based indexes.
Parallel branches and joins

Multiple eligible success transitions start parallel branches. When all branches converge on a shared activity, Run, Debug, and Python exports wait for the branches and execute that shared activity once. Nested forks join at their own convergence before reaching an enclosing join. Partial joins also wait for their participating branches: if two of three branches merge first, that intermediate activity runs once before its result joins the third branch. An unhandled branch failure prevents the shared continuation; Run and Python exports let sibling branches settle before reporting the failure. Debug steps branches individually and applies the same join barrier.

Each branch retains the task input and receives its own flow value and variables. Activity outputs remain available for explicit downstream mappings. The default value at a join comes from the last branch in transition order, independent of completion timing; business objects are not implicitly merged.

For example, connect Kafka and Pub/Sub branches to the same EMS activity to send to EMS after both complete. If EMS is instead a third outgoing branch, it runs in parallel and the common continuation waits for all three. Completion follows each connector's settings: Kafka `waitForDelivery=true` waits for broker acknowledgement; `false` completes after local enqueue. Regenerate deployed Python archives after upgrading Studio's execution behavior.

Engine-backed Python archives select connector modules from the packaged activities and groups instead of copying every engine file. All included Sub Tasks participate in selection, and JDBC transaction groups include the JDBC adapter. The exporter follows adapter imports transitively (including Java bridge dependencies and the JDBC adapter's Snowflake support). Shared scheduling, model, mapping/expression, and timestamp modules remain in every engine-backed archive. Optional connectors load only when executed; unused shared connection definitions do not cause their connector modules to be bundled. Standard JSON-based EAR archives do not contain this Python engine.

Direct archives are capability-linked from the persisted project model and selected task closure. The linker never checks project names, sample identifiers, known canvas layouts, or a catalog of previously exported applications. It records the exact activity operations and group types in `application/capabilities.py`, removes unreachable execution branches, specializes connector functions to the operations used by the project, and omits unreferenced activity modules, connector modules, native adapters, inbound servers, shared resources, schemas, and properties. Referenced shared resources are followed transitively, as are XSD `schemaLocation` and JSON Schema `$ref` dependencies, so dependency pruning does not produce an incomplete package. Its registry is required to cover every activity operation advertised by the direct exporter; adding a future supported Studio activity without linker metadata fails the exporter and its coverage test instead of silently generating an incomplete application. A property-driven resource, schema, or SAP messaging-provider selection conservatively retains compatible candidates because the selected object can change between packaged environments. Packaging never removes something required by a selected environment merely to make the archive smaller.

For a successfully compiled direct archive, run `python exported.pympkg --task TASK_ID --input '{"key":"value"}'` on a standard Python host. No extraction or source edit is needed. Alternatively, extract the archive and use `python run.py` as a Python-script job entry point (including a Databricks Python script task); pass `--environment PROFILE` when multiple profiles are packaged, and `--task TASK_ID` for a single task. Without `--task`, the generated application runs the selected starters; receiver starters keep polling until stopped. If no environment is specified, the first packaged profile is used.

Run `python run.py --check` (or `python exported.pympkg --check`) in the target data plane before deployment. The generated preflight checks only the dependencies used by that application, returns machine-readable JSON, and exits with code `2` when a required package, Java runtime, or external project artifact is missing. The Control Plane manifest also exposes the preflight command and dependency inventory.

For qualification against real providers, run `python run.py --qualify-task TASK_ID --input '{"test":true}' --iterations 1000 --concurrency 10`. Optional thresholds include `--max-error-rate`, `--max-p95-ms`, and `--max-memory-growth-mb`; `--duration-seconds` turns the same command into a bounded soak test. The command exercises the actual exported task and produces JSON evidence containing throughput, success/failure counts, latency percentiles, bounded error samples, and Python memory growth. It exits with code `3` when a threshold fails. Provider failover is tested by running this command while performing an approved broker/database/SAP failover in the test environment.

Real connectors require runtime provisioning, not source edits. Set `MINA_JAVA_BRIDGE_HOME` to the installed Java bridge directory containing `classes`, and `MINA_DRIVER_HOME` to a directory containing `sap/` and/or `jms/` licensed vendor JARs. Rebuild the bridge from this source before deploying client-acknowledge JMS flows. Place the SAP JCo native library in the SAP driver directory or on the platform native library path. A Java runtime must be available via `MINA_JAVA` or `PATH`. Depending on the generated preflight inventory, install `aiokafka`, `google-cloud-pubsub` and `google-auth`, `openpyxl`, `paramiko`, `snowflake-connector-python`, `pika`, or `azure-servicebus`. Provide connection URLs, credentials, and target-network access through the selected environment profile or environment variables. Missing packages and artifacts are reported before application startup.

The direct export is not a blanket compatibility promise for every future Studio feature. Grouped parallel fan-out still requires an explicit top-level branch boundary because a deterministic in-group join is not represented in the saved graph. Live ECC/JCo, EMS/JMS provider, AMQP, Snowflake, failover, and soak results cannot be asserted without those systems; use the generated qualification command in the target test environment and retain its evidence before approving production. The automated suite covers hosted REST, JMS request/reply correlation, SAP-over-Kafka, mixed nested groups, mock/in-memory providers, SQLite transactions, and bridge compilation. The saved `order-integration` project passes direct compiler static validation, which is not itself a live SAP qualification. Export reports unsupported graph behavior instead of generating a package with silently different behavior.
Native and Java database prerequisites

Generated archive checks identify the selected JDBC adapter and connection mode. SQLite uses Python's built-in driver. PostgreSQL requires `psycopg`, MySQL/MariaDB requires `pymysql`, native Oracle requires `oracledb`, native SQL Server requires `pyodbc`, DB2 requires `ibm_db_dbi`, Databricks requires `databricks.sql`, and Snowflake requires `snowflake.connector`. The checks provide corresponding pip installation commands; native libraries and licensed vendor drivers may require separate provisioning.

Oracle and SQL Server in Java/JDBC mode declare Java/driver prerequisites rather than requiring their native Python adapter. Native-only flows do not acquire a Java prerequisite. Declared environment-property driver choices are considered when generating checks. Both formats use the same requirement logic.

Direct archives containing JDBC retain the Snowflake adapter helper so a native Snowflake JDBC selection has its implementation even without a separate Snowflake activity. This does not bundle the vendor connector or credentials. See the HTTP/database resource verification guide for the archive regression checks.
MINA build and distribution
Product outputs
MINA has three independently distributable components:
**Studio** — an Electron desktop IDE for Windows. It embeds the React designer and a packaged Python sidecar.
**Control Plane** — a Linux or Windows management plane for data planes, capabilities, applications, resources, access, observability, and package deployment.
**Runtime package** — a portable `.mpkg`, `.tar.gz`, or `.ear`-compatible archive produced by Studio for either an on-premises or Kubernetes data plane.
Windows installation progress

The assisted Windows installers display a checklist during setup. Studio lists the app, local runtime, and background worker. Control Plane lists the desktop app. The installer checks off the bundled components together after extraction, then marks Windows registration and shortcuts complete.
Build Studio on Windows
Prerequisites:
Windows 10 or Windows 11 x64
Node.js satisfying Vite's requirement (`20.19+` or `22.12+`)
Python 3.11 x64 available through the `py` launcher
Internet access on the build machine for the first dependency installation
Run from a normal PowerShell or Command Prompt. PowerShell is used internally by the npm build script, but installed Studio users do not need PowerShell, Node.js, or Python.

cd D:\Integration-tool\MINA\frontend
npm ci
npm run desktop:installer -- -Version 2.4.0
Output:
frontend\release\MINAStudio-2.4.0-Setup.exe

`-Version` is injected into Electron Builder at build time; `package.json` is not edited. It must be a semantic version. CI can set `$env:MINA_VERSION = '2.4.0'` and run `npm run desktop:installer` without passing the argument. When neither is supplied, the version in `frontend/package.json` is used as the fallback.

The installer is machine-wide. An administrator installs it once, then each user opens MINA Studio from their own Windows session. Setup serializes installation across sessions and asks the administrator to close Studio before replacing the shared copy. For 50 or more concurrent users, follow [Shared Windows host rollout](STUDIO_MULTIUSER_WINDOWS.md).
Useful development commands:

npm run desktop:dev       # Vite UI in an Electron window with the Python sidecar
npm run desktop:unpacked  # Build without creating the installer
npm run desktop:installer # Build the sidecar and final Setup.exe
Corporate TLS certificate or proxy

`UNABLE_TO_GET_ISSUER_CERT_LOCALLY` from npm and `CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED` from pip mean the build machine does not trust the CA used by an HTTPS-inspecting corporate proxy. This is download trust, not Windows executable signing. Obtain the organization's root and intermediate CA chain from IT as one PEM file. Do not commit the certificate to this repository.
Configure both Node/npm and Python/pip from PowerShell, then open a new terminal:

$ca = 'C:\Certificates\company-ca-chain.pem'
npm.cmd config set cafile "$ca" --location=user
npm.cmd config set strict-ssl true --location=user
py -3.11 -m pip config --user set global.cert "$ca"
[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable('NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS', $ca, 'User')
[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable('PIP_CERT', $ca, 'User')
For the current terminal, set the values as well:

$env:NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS = $ca
$env:PIP_CERT = $ca
$env:REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE = $ca

Keep SSL verification enabled. If the company requires an explicit proxy, obtain its URL from IT and additionally configure `npm config set https-proxy <proxy-url> --location=user`, `HTTPS_PROXY`, and `ELECTRON_GET_USE_PROXY=1`.

After a failed `npm ci`, close running Node/Electron processes and delete the incomplete `frontend\node_modules` directory before retrying. The desktop build script now stops at the first failed npm, pip, Electron, or PyInstaller command instead of reporting a misleading successful sidecar build.

The desktop runtime is built with Python 3.11. Install the standard x64 distribution from python.org; a Microsoft Store execution alias that appears in `py -0p` but cannot launch is not sufficient. If `backend\.venv` uses another Python version, the installer build now preserves it and creates a dedicated Python 3.11 environment under `backend\build\.venv311`. The AMQP 1.0 connector uses the prebuilt `python-qpid-proton-wheel` distribution because the upstream `python-qpid-proton` 0.40 source release does not provide a CPython 3.11 Windows wheel and otherwise requires Microsoft Visual C++ Build Tools. Before PyInstaller starts, the build imports every external connector module and fails if a package or native DLL is unavailable.

Database shared connections accept either the Studio host/port/database fields or vendor JDBC URLs and translate them to the corresponding native Python adapter. The packaged runtime includes adapters for SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL/MariaDB, Oracle, IBM Db2, Databricks SQL, Snowflake, and SQL Server. SQL Server additionally requires Microsoft ODBC Driver 18 (or 17) to be installed on the runtime machine; the Studio detects installed drivers and reports the available names. Databricks supports personal access tokens, OAuth machine-to-machine, and interactive OAuth user-to-machine authentication with SQL warehouse hostname, HTTP path, catalog, and schema configuration.
Real SAP ECC connections

SAP shared connections use the licensed SAP Java Connector (JCo). New SAP connections use the external adapter by default; the local mock remains available as an explicit design-time option. JCo is not included in the installer. Place `sapjco3.jar` and its matching `sapjco3.dll` in the configured SAP driver directory (or the default `C:\ProgramData\MINA Studio\drivers\sap`). No Python SAP package or separate NW RFC SDK installation is required.

The repository includes `requirements-sap.txt` as a reminder. The Java bridge loads JCo at runtime, so the JCo JAR and DLL remain outside source control and are reported in the connection-test response.
See [SAP_INTEGRATION.md](SAP_INTEGRATION.md) for the supported IDoc/ALE, RFC/BAPI, transaction, lifecycle, and production certification behavior.

Ensure the SDK's native library directory is on `PATH` before starting Studio. For an application-server connection, configure `ashost`, `sysnr`, `client`, `user`, and `passwd`; for a message-server/logon-group connection, configure `mshost`, `sysid`, `group`, `client`, `user`, and `passwd`. SNC connections additionally require the SNC partner name and SAP Cryptographic Library path. The Test Connection action calls `STFC_CONNECTION` and reports the native RFC error when authentication, routing, authorization, or network setup fails.

After PyInstaller finishes, the build launches that exact packaged runtime on an isolated loopback port and requires a successful `/api/health` response before Electron Builder is allowed to create an installer. Installed Studio startup writes the runtime path, bound port, stdout, stderr, spawn errors, and exit status to `%APPDATA%\MINA Studio\logs\runtime-startup.log`. Startup errors include the log path and its latest output. The Windows kernel assigns the desktop runtime port, and the Studio window authenticates to its own runtime.

The Windows Studio window opens while the local runtime starts and switches to the welcome screen after the runtime passes its health check. Launching Studio again in the same Windows profile brings the existing window forward. If startup is slow, the same log records elapsed time for the startup page, runtime readiness, and Studio page load.

The build compiles the complete backend with Python 3.11 before freezing it. PyInstaller then explicitly collects every module under the backend `app` package and verifies `app.main` both before and after freezing. This catches incompatible Python syntax early and avoids environment-dependent namespace/package discovery producing an executable that fails with `ModuleNotFoundError: app.main`.
The unpacked executable is:
frontend\release\win-unpacked\MINA Studio.exe

For production distribution, configure a company `.pfx` code-signing certificate through environment variables. A signing certificate is optional for producing an installer, but recommended for publisher identity and SmartScreen reputation:

$env:WIN_CSC_LINK = 'C:\Certificates\mina-signing.pfx'
$env:WIN_CSC_KEY_PASSWORD = '<password-from-secret-store>'
npm.cmd run desktop:installer

Do not put the certificate or password in `package.json` or source control. Electron Builder automatically discovers `WIN_CSC_LINK`/`WIN_CSC_KEY_PASSWORD` (and supports `CSC_LINK`/`CSC_KEY_PASSWORD` as fallbacks).
Build Control Plane on Windows

cd D:\Integration-tool\MINA
.\scripts\build-administrator.ps1 -Version 2.4.0
Or from the `frontend` directory:
npm run administrator:windows -- -Version 2.4.0
Outputs:

administrator\dist\MinaAdministrator\MinaAdministrator.exe
administrator\release\MinaAdministrator-2.4.0-Windows-x64.zip

The ZIP is a PyInstaller **one-directory** distribution. Copy or extract the complete `MinaAdministrator` directory, including its `_internal`, `web`, and `bin` content. Copying only `MinaAdministrator.exe` will not work reliably.
Run it:

$env:MINA_ADMIN_DATA_DIR = "D:\MINAAdmin\data"
& .\administrator\dist\MinaAdministrator\MinaAdministrator.exe
Open `http://localhost:9080`. To listen on a different address or port, set `MINA_ADMIN_HOST` and `MINA_ADMIN_PORT`.
Build and install Control Plane on Linux
Use the [Control Plane and Data Plane one-stop guide](LINUX_SETUP.md) for transfer packaging, INI configuration, installation and lifecycle commands.
Run Control Plane as a container

docker build -f Dockerfile.administrator --build-arg MINA_VERSION=2.4.0 -t mina-administrator:2.4.0 .
docker run -d --name mina-admin -p 9080:9080 \
  -v mina-admin-data:/var/lib/mina/administrator \
  mina-administrator:2.4.0
Create deployment packages in Studio
Open **Packaging** in Project Explorer or select **Package** on the ribbon. Configure:
Artifact name and version
Target: **On-premises Linux** or **Cloud / Kubernetes**
Target environment
Archive: `.mpkg`, `.tar.gz`, or `.ear`

An on-premises package contains an Administrator deployment descriptor. A cloud package contains a Docker build input and Kubernetes deployment manifest. Password property values are removed from both outputs and replaced by deployment-time secret requirements.

The `.mpackage` file is the editable Studio project package. The `.mpkg` file is the immutable deployment artifact. Studio and Control Plane continue accepting legacy `.ifproject`, `.ifpackage`, and `.ifpkg` files during the compatibility period.
Vendor Java connector bridge

Desktop builds require JDK 17 or newer (`javac` and `jlink`). The build bundles a minimal Java runtime automatically; target machines do not need Java installed. EMS, Microsoft SQL Server JDBC, and Oracle JDBC JAR placement is documented in [VENDOR_DRIVERS.md](VENDOR_DRIVERS.md).

pages.title: MINA Studio on a shared Windows host

blocks.text: MINA Studio on a shared Windows host

Use one machine-wide installation with a separate Windows account and private user profile for each developer. Each Studio starts a local runtime with an independent workspace, Run state, Debug sessions, and logs. Installed binaries are shared. The runtime reserves its own Windows-assigned loopback port and accepts Studio API calls only with the credential for that launch.
Host rollout

The host administrator installs `MINAStudio-<version>-Setup.exe` once from a maintenance session. Close Studio in every active Windows session before setup, upgrades, or uninstall. Ask users to save their work and close Studio normally. A concurrent setup request exits while the first owns the installer lock.

Give users standard Windows accounts, private profiles and sufficient storage for `%APPDATA%\MINA Studio\workspace-data` and the profile's logs and caches. If using profile containers, verify that storage performance and access controls hold during a logon burst. Keep installation files read-only for standard users.

Have each user launch **MINA Studio** from the Start menu in their own desktop session. Open their own source-control working copy or save imported projects under their private workspace. Exchange work through source control or project exports. Grant shared resources only to users who need them.

Give hosted Run and Debug HTTP services distinct host/port assignments per developer when they are used concurrently. Set a project environment property for the HTTP server connection's port and give each developer a different local value from an administrator-approved range. Use loopback bindings for local tests and configure authentication for hosted listeners when their data must be private. The Studio API credential is separate from the hosted application's authentication.

For broker and database development, provision separate test consumer groups, queues/subscriptions, database schemas and credentials where developers need isolation. Peak resource demand depends on the project, payload sizes, connector clients and concurrent listeners.
Capacity and acceptance test

Run the sidecar soak on a nonproduction representative host. The harness starts 52 isolated runtime processes, verifies unique ports and checks that anonymous calls and the next user's credential are rejected. It runs concurrent project saves and reads, Run calls, interactive Debug steps, and trace reads. Every user uses the same project identifier to expose accidental cross-profile reuse. On Windows the report also samples private memory and working sets for the test sidecars.
From the repository root, using the installer build environment with Python 3.11 and `httpx`:

& .\backend\build\.venv311\Scripts\python.exe .\scripts\studio-multiuser-soak.py --users 52 --seconds 600 --live-http --runtime ".\frontend\release\win-unpacked\resources\runtime\MINARuntime\MINARuntime.exe" --output ".\tmp\studio-multiuser\report.json"

The `--live-http` option adds an actual HTTP Run listener and Debug listener per runtime and checks that each returns only its own fixture response. The script stops on functional or isolation failures. The default latency gate is 2,000 ms P95 for each measured API operation. Its temporary data stays under its output directory and is removed after the run. Logs for real Studio launches are in each profile's `logs\runtime-startup.log`.

The soak separates designer asset loading, project creation, and listener startup. All 52 users participate in each phase by default. On Windows, the test requests that the system stay awake during the run and releases that request when the test exits. The report includes load-driver event-loop delay and saves partial timings on transport or functional failure. It never retries a failed Run or Debug command. The optional `--provision-batch` setting stages project creation and listener startup while keeping all users active during the timed workload.

HTTP/1 listeners publish readiness after the socket is accepting connections. Anonymous HTTP routes skip authentication worker warmup and dispatch. Authenticated routes keep their configured worker policy. Studio Run, Debug, and HTTP preview move project reads and log writes off the network event loop.

Complete Windows host acceptance by launching Studio in at least 52 actual desktop sessions on the target host, opening representative projects, and repeating saves, Run, Debug, and live listener operations. Check user-visible response time, CPU, memory, profile-disk throughput, and external connector limits. The sidecar report covers the server workload and generated designer assets. Full desktop capacity also depends on Electron renderers, RDS, and the host's OS and policies.
Vendor driver installation
MINA Studio bundles its own minimal Java runtime and connector bridge. Vendor-licensed JARs are intentionally not distributed in the installer.

Vendor native client libraries (`.lib`, `.dll`, `.so`, `.dylib`) and license keys are also external prerequisites. They are ignored by Git under `drivers/`, and artifact verification rejects known SAP/EMS/JMS binaries in release payloads. Keep local drivers in the configured driver folder; source cleanup must not delete customer-owned local copies. See [distribution compliance](../compliance/README.md) for release SBOMs, notices and remaining permission/source-access review.
The default machine-wide driver root on Windows is:
C:\ProgramData\MINA Studio\drivers

Set `MINA_DRIVER_HOME` to override the complete root, or enter a **Driver JAR directory** in an individual shared connection. Source checkouts also search `D:\Integration-tool\MINA\drivers` as a development fallback.
EMS / JMS

Place the provider's EMS client and the matching JMS API JAR in the `jms` directory under the driver root. If the provider requires a separate library for failover, install the matching version from the same distribution.

In Direct mode, set the server URL and the provider's fully qualified connection factory class. In JNDI mode, set the provider URL, the initial context factory class, and the connection factory lookup name. Supply credentials if your provider requires them.
Microsoft SQL Server
Download the Microsoft JDBC Driver for SQL Server and place the Java 11-compatible JAR in:
C:\ProgramData\MINA Studio\drivers\jdbc\sqlserver\mssql-jdbc-<version>.jre11.jar

The driver class is `com.microsoft.sqlserver.jdbc.SQLServerDriver`. SQL Server Authentication is fully Java-based and does not need ODBC. Windows Integrated Authentication additionally requires Microsoft's architecture-matched authentication DLL; username/password authentication is the portable default.
Oracle Database
Place the Oracle JDBC driver in:
C:\ProgramData\MINA Studio\drivers\jdbc\oracle\ojdbc11.jar

Optional Oracle companion JARs such as `orai18n.jar`, `ucp.jar`, or Oracle PKI libraries can be put in the same directory when the selected Oracle features require them. The driver class is `oracle.jdbc.OracleDriver`. Thin JDBC mode does not require Oracle Instant Client.
Build prerequisite
The installer build machine needs JDK 17 or newer because `desktop:installer` compiles the bridge and creates the bundled Java runtime. End-user machines do not need Java installed.
Build the bridge alone with:
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\build-java-bridge.ps1
The connection-test response reports `loadedJars`, making it possible to verify exactly which vendor files were loaded.
MINA environment variables

This is the reference list of environment variables recognized by the current MINA source, Studio sidecar, and Control Plane. Variable names are case-sensitive on Linux and Kubernetes. Values containing passwords, private keys, API keys, or tokens must be supplied by the operating system, service manager, or cloud secret store; do not commit them to a project or container image.
Runtime and Studio sidecar

rows: Backend HTTP port used by `run_sidecar.py`. Installed Studio requests port `0` so the operating system binds an available loopback port.
Uvicorn process log level, for example `debug`, `info`, `warning`, or `error`.
Runtime data root for projects, SAP TID files, and default project logs.
Process-wide fallback log root when `runtime.logDirectory` is blank.
Maximum size of each project log file before rotation.
Number of rotated project log files retained.
IANA display timezone for runtime, debugger, and audit timestamps. Arizona is emitted with `-07:00`.
Runtime worker-thread setting; otherwise environment property `advanced.workerThreads` or `advanced.threadCount` is used.

Windows only: maximum simultaneous SSH transport workers per runtime process/module, from 1 to 128. Lazy persistent workers bound native cryptography thread state. Excess connections wait up to their configured timeout, then fail without closing other sessions. Set before the first SFTP connection and restart after changes. Connections and credentials are not pooled.
Application directory supplied to a deployed runtime by the Control Plane.
Deployment identifier supplied by the Control Plane.
Runtime instance identifier supplied by the Control Plane.
Build/version value included in startup diagnostics.
Override location of backend-served frontend assets.
SAP JCo/native driver directory override. Must contain matching `sapjco3.jar` and native library.
Java executable override for the SAP/JMS Java bridge.
AI Builder model name when `OPENAI_API_KEY` is configured.
Enables the OpenAI AI Builder provider. Store as a secret.

blocks.text: The Electron Studio sets `MINA_PORT`, `MINA_DATA_DIR`, `MINA_LOG_LEVEL`, and `MINA_BUILD_VERSION` for its child runtime. It also supports these Studio-only process variables:

rows: Python executable override for development sidecar startup.
Frontend development URL loaded by Electron instead of the local production URL.

blocks.text: Control Plane

rows: Control Plane state root: packages, deployments, machines, secrets, audit, and logs. Mount this directory persistently.
Technology Team API key. When set, protected APIs require `X-Admin-Key` or `X-Control-Plane-Key`. Store in a secret manager.
Stable encryption key for stored deployment secrets. Required from a durable secret store for production and clustered deployments.
Trusted command template used to start an on-premises runtime. Supports `{application}`, `{package}`, `{environment}`, `{deployment_id}`, and `{instance_id}`.
Maximum uploaded package size in megabytes.
Maximum expanded package size in megabytes.
Override location of Control Plane frontend files.

blocks.text: The Linux service wrapper also recognizes:
Build and packaging variables

rows: Default version passed to Studio or Control Plane build scripts when no explicit version argument is supplied.
Windows Electron signing certificate and password. Keep both outside source control.
Electron Builder fallback names for Windows signing.

blocks.text: `MINA_VERSION` and signing variables are build-time settings; they are not needed on an installed runtime machine.
Automatically injected deployment variables

When the Control Plane starts an on-premises deployment, it injects `MINA_APPLICATION_DIR`, `MINA_ENVIRONMENT`, `MINA_DEPLOYMENT_ID`, and `MINA_INSTANCE_ID`. It also injects the deployment's decrypted secret values using their configured names. These values should not be manually duplicated in a package or checked into source control.
Windows
For the current PowerShell session:

$env:MINA_DATA_DIR = 'C:\ProgramData\MINA\runtime-data'
$env:MINA_RUNTIME_LOG_DIR = 'D:\IntegrationLogs'
$env:MINA_LOG_TIMEZONE = 'America/Phoenix'
$env:MINA_DRIVER_HOME = 'C:\SAP\jco'
python -m uvicorn app.main:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8787

For a persistent machine-level setting, run PowerShell as Administrator and use `[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable('NAME', 'VALUE', 'Machine')`. Restart the service or application after changing environment variables.
Linux and systemd
Create a root-readable environment file such as `/etc/mina/runtime.env`:

MINA_DATA_DIR=/opt/mina/runtime/data
MINA_RUNTIME_LOG_DIR=/opt/mina/logs/runtime
MINA_LOG_TIMEZONE=America/Phoenix
MINA_DRIVER_HOME=/opt/mina/drivers
MINA_ENVIRONMENT=dev
Reference it from the service unit:

[Service]
EnvironmentFile=/etc/mina/runtime.env
Protect files containing secrets with `chmod 600` and set the service account as owner. Run `systemctl daemon-reload` and restart the service after changes.
Docker and Kubernetes
Use ordinary configuration values for paths and ports, and use Docker/Kubernetes Secrets for credentials:

env:
  - name: MINA_ENVIRONMENT
    value: dev
  - name: MINA_LOG_TIMEZONE
    value: America/Phoenix
  - name: MINA_DATA_DIR
    value: /var/lib/mina/runtime
  - name: MINA_ADMIN_API_KEY
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef:
        name: mina-admin-secrets
        key: api-key
  - name: MINA_ADMIN_SECRET_KEY
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef:
        name: mina-admin-secrets
        key: encryption-key

Persist `MINA_DATA_DIR` and `MINA_ADMIN_DATA_DIR` on volumes. For SAP JCo, provide the licensed matching JCo JAR/native library through a protected volume or image layer and set `MINA_DRIVER_HOME` to that directory. Do not print secret environment values in startup diagnostics.
Operational notes
Environment variables are read during process startup; restart the affected
process after changing them.
Relative paths are resolved from the process/application data location and
should be replaced with absolute paths in production.
`MINA_LOG_TIMEZONE` changes display timestamps only. Scheduler and token
expiry calculations continue to use UTC internally.
Existing log files are not rewritten when the timezone changes.
To inspect effective non-secret settings on Windows use `Get-ChildItem Env:`;
on Linux use `env` or `systemctl show <service> --property=Environment`.
SAP ECC integration runtime guide

MINA uses the licensed SAP Java Connector (JCo) supplied by the customer. The connector is not redistributed with Studio. This implementation interoperates with SAP ECC through public RFC/JCo contracts. MINA is an independent product and does not include third-party proprietary connector implementations.

MINA itself is **not SAP-certified** merely because it uses JCo. SAP permits JCo to connect external applications to SAP in both directions, but the customer must download it from SAP, comply with named-user/solution licensing, and must not redistribute the connector. Record the JCo, Java, OS, and CPU architecture reported by Test Connection as part of every production approval.
Supported integration patterns

rows: Persistent registered JCo server, tRFC TID duplicate protection, bounded delivery queue, one workflow per IDoc in a package, enclosing transaction commit only after every IDoc succeeds
Persistent registered JCo server for the selected function, request/reply export and table response mapping, rollback when the task fails or omits Reply
Persistent, bounded JVM worker pool; JCo destination pooling; import, changing, nested structure, and table parameters; request/reply, tRFC, and qRFC transport
XML or rendered input is converted to EDI_DC40 and EDI_DD40 and sent with `IDOC_INBOUND_ASYNCHRONOUS`; tRFC or qRFC is selected at transport level
Metadata-driven, byte-position fixed-width conversion with physical E2 to logical E1 normalization, configurable code page, strict/replace invalid-byte policy, and delimiter-safe flat records
`RFC_READ_TABLE` field, filter, paging, and named-record output
A dedicated persistent JVM and thread-bound JCo context across activities; explicit commit/end, rollback on failure/expiry, bounded session count, and duplicate-session rejection
Invokes the customer-configured SAP acknowledgment RFC because this function is solution-specific

blocks.text: ALE distribution is implemented through the IDoc listener/posting paths. SAP partner profiles, ports, process codes, message types, RFC destinations, and authorizations remain SAP Basis configuration and are not generated by Studio.
Required runtime files
Install a matching x64 JCo distribution in one of these locations:

C:\ProgramData\MINA Studio\drivers\sap\sapjco3.jar
C:\ProgramData\MINA Studio\drivers\sap\sapjco3.dll

On Linux use `libsapjco3.so` next to `sapjco3.jar`, or select an explicit SAP driver directory in the shared connection. The packaged Java runtime and JCo native library must have the same architecture. Do not mix files from different JCo releases.

Use a currently supported SAP JCo 3.1 patch and a JDK/JRE listed for that patch in SAP Note 2786882. As of September 2026 SAP publishes JCo 3.1.14 and lists Java 8, 11, 17, 21, and 25; re-check SAP's support page when qualifying a build.
ECC configuration checklist
Create the RFC user with only the required S_RFC and IDoc authorizations.
Configure SM59 for the Studio Program ID, gateway host, and gateway service.
Configure WE21, WE20, message types, process codes, and partner profiles for
ALE/IDoc traffic.
For qRFC, configure and monitor the queue in SMQ1/SMQ2 and set a non-empty
SAP queue name in the activity.
Make each concurrently deployed registered server identity unambiguous.
Keep the TID store on durable writable storage. Never share one TID file
between unrelated Program IDs.
Validate `STFC_CONNECTION`, fetch the actual IDoc/RFC metadata, and save the
selected metadata with the project before packaging.
Resource and failure behavior
Listener event queues and stderr history are bounded. Backpressure reaches
the JCo callback instead of permitting unbounded Python heap growth.
Cancellation does not leave blocked Python executor threads. Runtime shutdown
closes native listener processes and removes their temporary descriptors.
The JCo server waits for the workflow result. Success commits the delivery;
task failure, cancellation, missing RFC Reply, or reply timeout rolls it back so SAP can retry according to its transaction policy.
TID state is persisted atomically. A previously committed or in-flight TID is
rejected as a duplicate; SAP confirmation removes it.
Single-call BAPI auto-commit executes `BAPI_TRANSACTION_COMMIT` in the same
JCo context as the BAPI call.
A Dynamic Connection with `transactional=true` pins all calls carrying its

`sessionID` to one worker/JCo context. `contextEnd=true` closes the context; with `autoCommit=true` it first executes `BAPI_TRANSACTION_COMMIT`. Failure, expiry, or normal termination without `commitOnTerminate=true` rolls back.
External outbound calls use persistent JVM workers. `outboundWorkerCount`

controls Python-side worker concurrency; `poolCapacity`, `peakLimit`, and `connectionExpirationMilliseconds` configure the JCo destination pool in each worker. Changing any connection setting, including credentials, creates a distinct pool identity without storing plaintext credentials in its key.
Flat IDoc and messaging modes

In JSON mode, the IDoc Parser and Converter expose one schema-shaped document under `SAPIDoc`, for example `SAPIDoc.ARTMAS05.IDOC`. Map `SAPIDoc` to a Kafka JSON payload to send that document once. Older direct runtime mapping paths such as `SAPIDoc.IDOC` and `ARTMAS05.IDOC` remain available as lookup aliases; they are not additional serialized JSON branches. Actual repeating IDocs and segments remain in the payload.

The built-in parser reads canonical EDI_DD40 byte fields (`SEGNAM`, `MANDT`, `DOCNUM`, `SEGNUM`, `PSGNUM`, `HLEVEL`, and `SDATA`) and EDI_DC40 control fields. Set `idocEncoding` to the actual sender code page. Keep `invalidCharacterPolicy=strict` for production unless replacement characters are an accepted business rule. When SDATA may contain CR/LF, configure a unique `idocRecordDelimiter`; that delimiter is authoritative and embedded line breaks remain data. With no delimiter, canonical 1063-byte records are split by width.

If the separately licensed `sapidoc3.jar` is installed, Test Connection reports its presence and version. Selecting the SAP JIDocLib parser engine validates IDoc XML with SAP's repository-backed `IDocXMLProcessor`; flat EDI_DD40 input continues to use the built-in byte parser because SAP documents the public IDoc class-library processor as an XML processor.
IDoc Listener supports these sources:
`NoMessaging`: the direct persistent JCo RFC server, including durable TID
handling and SAP transaction acknowledgment.
`EMS` or `JMS`: consumes one queue message through the selected shared
connection and publishes its body to the parser. Client acknowledgment is exposed through the standard Confirm Message activity.
`Kafka`: consumes one topic record through the selected Kafka resource and
publishes its value to the parser. Manual offset confirmation uses the same Confirm Message contract.

For broker-backed modes, select `messagingResourceId` and `messagingDestination`. SAP-to-broker transaction atomicity is owned by the upstream bridge; MINA does not claim an XA transaction spanning SAP tRFC and an independent EMS/JMS/Kafka broker.
Production certification

Unit and mock tests verify serialization, lifecycle, transaction routing, and bounded queues, but they cannot certify a particular ECC/JCo combination. Before production, run an environment test with the exact JCo version and architecture:
sustained IDoc batches containing the largest expected SDATA payloads;
concurrent RFC/BAPI calls at the configured maximum connection count;
SAP and Studio restart during in-flight tRFC/qRFC deliveries;
duplicate TID, reply timeout, malformed IDoc, network partition, and expired
credential scenarios;
a 24-72 hour soak while recording process RSS, JVM heap/GC, thread count,
handle count, queue depth, throughput, and SAP SM58/SMQ1/SMQ2 state.
Do not accept the connector for production until those measurements remain stable and every failed transaction is demonstrably recoverable.
The repository includes a repeatable qualification runner and an intentionally non-secret example configuration:

Copy-Item docs\sap-soak-config.example.json sap-soak-config.local.json
# Edit the local copy with QA-only credentials and parameters, then run:
backend\.venv\Scripts\python.exe scripts\sap-production-soak.py `
  --config sap-soak-config.local.json --output sap-soak-report.json

Set `terminateWorkerEveryCalls` to a positive number for controlled worker-JVM failure injection. Run separate 24–72 hour profiles for sRFC, transactional BAPI and tRFC/qRFC IDoc posting. To qualify the 10-minute outbound target, set `durationSeconds` to `600` and add `--target-calls 100000`. The report fails if the 100,000th successful call falls after the deadline or a call fails. The report holds throughput, failures, latency percentiles, and worker process IDs; correlate those IDs with OS/JVM monitoring and SAP SM58/SMQ1/SMQ2 evidence. Never commit the local configuration because it contains credentials.
Qualifying SAP IDoc Listener throughput

Studio times the complete IDoc Parser activity, including connection settings and input mappings. Fetched IDoc catalogs are treated as metadata, and their fields are reused across executions. For XML inputs, the parser builds one tree and uses it directly to produce JSON. When XML output is selected, the parser serializes the expanded tree once. For a performance comparison, replay the same document, output mode, task, and Debug settings. Collect a separate live measurement for gateway and downstream provider timings.

The listener splits SAP packages by document number. Each callback waits for all document workflows in the package. MINA reports a failed callback if a document fails or if queue admission and workflow acknowledgements exceed the configured `ackTimeoutSeconds`. SAP may replay the package, so use the document number and business context for idempotency at downstream systems. The bridge records its first inbound IDoc package and every thousandth package thereafter, plus callback errors and startup diagnostics.

Use **Execution analytics → SAP IDoc deliveries** to compare document numbers and SAP transaction IDs against the sender's list. In Run, the section shows the outcome of each recorded delivery within the latest 100 workflow runs. In Debug, it shows receipts in the current Debug log. The **Activity analysis** table records one IDoc Listener invocation per receipt in Run and Debug. Listener time measures local processing once a document is available, including native SAP payload conversion and handoff to the workflow. It excludes idle wait for SAP, acknowledgement, and downstream steps. **Activity invocations** counts the listener and downstream calls. The HTML and JSON execution reports include the delivery list. For older deliveries, use the project runtime logs and search for `sap-idoc`. Bridge callback errors are shown even when SAP sends no later document. An unsplit or malformed batch is rejected so SAP can retry it.

The 10-minute target requires at least 166.7 completed documents per second. On approved QA, send 100,000 unique IDocs with representative sizes from SAP and verify downstream completions and SAP transaction confirmations within 600 seconds. Include the real downstream activities. Compare SAP packaging, RFC registration count (`maximumConnections`), MINA workflow concurrency (`maxConcurrentIdocs`, defaulting to the connection count), gateway limits, disk latency, and the slowest downstream activity. Use one active listener per registered Program ID on a host. Benchmark RFC/BAPI operations separately in calls per second and distinguish them from IDocs per second. At eight workers, sustaining the IDoc target requires a mean worker time below 48 ms even before accounting for idle time.

The replay test exercises Listener → Parser → End with synthetic bridge events and checks unique document numbers, segment values, and acknowledgements. With backend dependencies installed, set `MINA_SAP_REPLAY_RECORDS=100000` and run `python -m unittest discover -s backend/tests -p test_sap_idoc_throughput.py` with `backend` on `PYTHONPATH`. It covers Studio Run and both Python exports. The Java bridge test takes the document count as an argument and checks package splitting, transaction duplicates, rollback, and restart behavior. Live SAP gateway, native library, network, and downstream timings require the QA run.
The Windows development workspace recorded these synthetic results on November 19, 2026. Each test checked 100,000 documents.
